To structurally isolate macro-exploration from micro-exploitation, Level 3 encapsulates an autonomous Elite Memory Archive that preserves high-fidelity sub-schemas and hosts a discrete bitwise Differential Evolution (DE) micro-refinement sandbox for resolving complex parameter epistasis. Theoretically, uniform combinatorial bounds derived via Vapnik--Chervonenkis (VC) dimension criteria demonstrate that this multi-level restriction mitigates high-dimensional overfitting. Empirical results across manifolds scaling up to $d > 100{,}000$ features, complemented by high-performance computing (HPC) profiling under lock-free atomic Compare-and-Swap (CAS) primitives, indicate strong performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines. The framework exhibits near-linear parallel speedups, sub-quadratic runtime scaling, and substantial dimensionality reduction, offering a scalable and structurally innovative paradigm for large-scale data mining.
  </details>

- **[Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01135)**  `arXiv:2611.01135`  
  _Zhengshuai Yang, Changyun Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.
  </details>

- **[HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01129)**  `arXiv:2611.01129`  
  _Zhuohang Jiang, Yuxin Chen, Haohao Qu, ZeFei luo, Yunlong Wang, Xu Yuan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.
  </details>

- **[Robust Reward Machine Learning and Execution in Noisy Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01063)**  `arXiv:2611.01063`  
  _Roko Parac, Lorenzo Nodari, Daniel Furelos-Blanco, Leo Ardon, Federico Cerutti, Alessandra Russo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Background: Reward machines (RMs) represent non-Markovian reward functions as finite-state machines over high-level propositional events. Traditionally, these events are generated by a deterministic labelling function that maps environment states to proposition sets. However, real-world labelling functions are inherently noisy.Objectives: Design and implement a method that learns RMs in the presence of noisy labelling functions and exploits them for policy learning in both discrete and continuous environments.Methods: We propose Prob-IRM, a method that learns RMs from noisy proposition histories using inductive logic programming (ILP) and exploits them for policy learning. Noisy proposition histories are represented as training examples for ILP, which learns an RM that maximises coverage of low-uncertainty histories. RM learning is interleaved with policy optimisation. Prob-IRM uses a belief over RM states to determine when to relearn the RM and to provide additional guiding rewards.Results: Prob-IRM is evaluated on environments with discrete and continuous state spaces under varying levels of labelling noise. Prob-IRM performs comparably to baselines using handcrafted RMs and outperforms approaches that use recurrent neural networks to encode history, despite operating with noisy labels.Conclusions: Prob-IRM represents a step towards deploying reward machines in noisy, real-world environments.
  </details>

- **[Appointed-Time Fault-Tolerant Fast Terminal Sliding Control for UAVs with a Tracking Error-Based Disturbance Observer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01061)**  `arXiv:2611.01061`  
  _Jinfa Li, Sheng Xu, Yanjie Wu, Chengyue Su_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper addresses the critical challenge of high-performance fault-tolerant tracking control for quadrotor UAVs under complex conditions including external disturbances, parameter uncertainties, and actuator faults. A synergistic control framework is proposed by decoupling the system into position and attitude loops, each governed by the following three innovations. First, an Appointed-Time Prescribed Performance Function (AT-PPF) is developed to strictly constrain the tracking error within a predefined funnel boundary, ensuring convergence within a fixed time regardless of initial conditions. Second, a Tracking Error-Based Fixed-Time Composite Disturbance Observer (TFxTCDO) is developed to enable fast and accurate estimation of lumped disturbances without requiring full-state information or precise system modeling. This observer directly couples disturbance estimation with the control objective, thereby enhancing robustness and convergence. Third, a Fast Second-Order Terminal Sliding Mode Controller (NFSO-TSMC) is designed to achieve faster convergence and effective chattering mitigation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed control strategy significantly outperforms conventional methods in terms of tracking accuracy, fault recovery speed, and robustness against uncertainties.
  </details>

- **[Temperature, Not Knowledge: What Recursive Self-Training and Its Remedies Do to a Language Model's Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01059)**  `arXiv:2611.01059`  
  _Dipto Sumit, Syeda Fabiayee Jahan, Farig Sadeque_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recursive self-training can collapse language models, and many proposed remedies target overconfidence, yet their effects on confidence are rarely measured. We study a five-round self-training loop on Qwen3-1.7B, using three seeds per compared method, and distinguish confidence temperature (drift from a calibrated starting point) from discrimination (ranking correct answers above incorrect ones). Accuracy and overall discrimination remain nearly unchanged, but confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable. Matching predictive entropy to the calibrated starting model each round recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, at both 1.7B and 8B. Sharpening is not inherent to self-training: exact samples from a model's distribution have zero expected gradient. Instead, most drift comes from fitting each generated answer twice, with top-p truncation contributing the rest; removing both keeps entropy on generated outputs flat. Remedies affect the two properties differently: truncated cross-entropy, an entropy bonus, and single-pass training preserve temperature without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but cause underconfidence. Reference-data mixing also overshoots. Pairing a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both.
  </details>

- **[Constraint Dependency Graph Retrieval for Compliance Detection on Long SKILL Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01042)**  `arXiv:2611.01042`  
  _Shuaitao Zhao, Feng Ni, Lichao Ma, Yuchen Wei, Shuaike Li, Jiaye Lin, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Model (LLM) agents carry out business operations under enterprise documents we refer to as SKILL documents, which take the form of standard operating procedures (SOPs) that state the conditions to verify and the actions to take before an operation proceeds. Long, densely cross-referenced SKILL documents exceed the context budget of small deployed auditors. Similarity-based retrieval then brings in irrelevant rules while omitting mandatory prerequisites, and the two-stage audit policy provides no trainable signal for the retrieval stage. We present SkillCDG, a compliance detection framework that reformulates each SKILL document as a constraint dependency graph, shifting rule retrieval from similarity-based matching to closure-based selection under the deployment's context budget. Each atomic rule is anchored to its source text span as a graph node, and mandatory prerequisite relations form the sole edge type. Policy-generated retrieval keywords activate seed rules, whose dependency closure yields a compact and conditionally complete rule context within that budget. The same graph also supports a joint optimization scheme. The retrieval stage is trained with group-relative policy optimization using a verifiable reward that combines output-format validity with downstream verdict correctness, with closure non-emptiness serving as a validity gate, while selective on-policy distillation concentrates teacher supervision on high-entropy reasoning tokens, with verdict and termination tokens always included, to improve verdict accuracy. Experiments on three enterprise datasets and two public benchmarks show that SkillCDG improves accuracy and F1 over the full-document and retrieval-based baselines.
  </details>

- **[IJev: Order-Invariant Decisions via Iterated Cyclic Reordering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01015)**  `arXiv:2611.01015`  
  _Youzhi Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  System One decision models answer a choice question in one forward pass, but their answer depends on the order in which options are listed, and their probabilities carry a prior over answer labels. An invariant ordering operator is any fixed function that returns the same ordered option list for every input order of a fixed option set. Starting from any such order and averaging a listwise readout over its K cyclic shifts removes the input order, but the decision still depends on the chosen cyclic class: those $K$ shifts are only one of the (K-1)! classes, and different invariant operators can select different classes. We propose IJev, which repeatedly reorders the options by the cyclic-averaged, label-prior-corrected distribution and runs another cyclic average. Every iterate is exactly input-order-invariant. When the iteration does not converge, we average the round distributions rather than return the last round. On five benchmarks and five models, IJev has flip rate zero in every cell. The default uniform average over T=20 rounds substantially improves calibration over a single cyclic average, and its accuracy is comparable. A descriptive choice of horizon and averaging rule is best or tied-best for accuracy in all 25 settings.
  </details>

- **[Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01011)**  `arXiv:2611.01011`  
  _Lin Yang, Yunjie Shen, Zheyu Li, Zhenjie Tian, Yongli Wang, Dongze Huang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $\tau$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.
  </details>

- **[Pulse: Long-Horizon Tasks Need Streaming Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00988)**  `arXiv:2611.00988`  
  _Qijia Zhuang, Jialiang Liang, Yuxiang Ren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $\pi$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
  </details>

- **[Benchmarking Machine-Learning Classifiers for Neoantigen Immunogenicity Prediction and the Limits of SHAP Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00907)**  `arXiv:2611.00907`  
  _Ramon Gonzalez_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Personalized cancer vaccines require prioritizing, among hundreds of candidate mutant peptides, the few that will induce a T-cell response. This study asks what general-purpose machine learning achieves on that task, and whether the features such models identify as important can be trusted.We make three contributions. The first is a benchmark of sixty models: twelve supervised classifier families, each in five configurations, evaluated on the Immunogenic Tumor Specific Neoantigen database (ITSNdb; 199 experimentally validated neoantigens, 129 immunogenic and 70 non-immunogenic). All sixty are compared under one stratified k-fold cross-validation protocol, in which the data used to choose a configuration are never the data used to score it. The second is an interpretability study that combines SHAP with feature ablation. The third is a shuffled-label control that tests whether a SHAP value has been earned.Two results follow, and both run against current practice. First, the classical linear models lead the ranking. The gradient-boosted ensembles and neural networks that dominate recent work bring no advantage. Second, SHAP can fail on high-cardinality categorical features. Ablation establishes the presenting HLA allele as the dominant input and the source gene as dispensable. SHAP reports the opposite, assigning 68.7% to 81.7% of its total value to the source gene in every model that gives each gene its own weight. Shuffling the gene labels at random among the peptides resolves the contradiction: the meaningless column earns the same SHAP value as the real one. That value measures only that ITSNdb contains 173 genes for 199 peptides. We therefore recommend that SHAP values for high-cardinality categorical annotations in cohorts of this size always be reported against such a shuffled-label control, and we describe one in full.
  </details>

- **[VCoT-SQL: Enhancing Text-to-SQL Generation through Dual Chain-of-Thought Validation Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00815)**  `arXiv:2611.00815`  
  _Rui Zhang, Yujia Su, Ruixuan Li, Yuhua Li, Yixin Su_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Open-source LLMs provide a flexible alternative to closed-source models for Text-to-SQL but still struggle with complex queries. Finetuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) data improves reasoning, yet standard datasets lack CoT annotations, requiring synthetic generation. Existing synthesis methods only verify the final answer, allowing flawed reasoning steps to corrupt the training data. We propose VCoT-SQL, a framework that improves Text-to-SQL generation through intermediate-step validated CoT supervision and a dedicated SQL validator, which enables small open-source models to outperform frontier closed-source models. VCoT-SQL trains two complementary models on curated reasoning traces: an SQL generator using clause-level CoT templates where reasoning steps are verified via execution and schema alignment checks, and an SQL validator using diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic, and type level errors. We further design a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline that integrates and refines complementary retrieval strategies to distill relevant database elements. VCoT-SQL achieves 66.82% execution accuracy on challenging dataset BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD. Notably, our CoT synthesis relies on 7B models yet outperforms methods that use 72B-scale or even proprietary closed source teachers for data generation, demonstrating that rigorous step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up teacher model size. Our dataset and code are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[AI Data Analysis: A New Approach - Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00807)**  `arXiv:2611.00807`  
  _Jean Ye_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  AI data analysis today is three fragmented worlds: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute; BI aggregates precisely but is stateless; ML processes large-scale data on a stateful kernel but lacks semantics. This paper proposes a combination mechanism, named Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, that fills a still-open gap - the multi-engine joint context: the data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis, where the LLM serves only as the semantic, reasoning, and orchestration layer (not computation) and connects four engines through the 1M context window - Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases, Cypher over graph databases - yielding two multiplications, "semantics and precise computation" and "relational and graph", under enterprise-grade governance. The novelty is a four-dimensional coordinate system: horizontal (engine kinds), vertical (state flow - the watershed), spatial (business generalization), temporal (iterative convergence); a deterministic grounding method (one-shot injection ofthis http URL+this http URL, M+S) carries the spatial and temporal dimensions. Empirically, all four dimensions are substantiated: horizontally, four engines are quantified - SQL, Cypher (96.5% on CypherBench movie), ML in Python and R (TabReD weather); vertically, state flows across engines and grounding is reused across kernels; spatially, SQL generalizes across three business databases - AdventureWorks 91.3%, financial 95.3%, formula_1 94.6% (average), about 20-23 points above single-shot SOTA 74.45%; temporally, accuracy converges monotonically as notes accumulate. The core invariant - the separation of semantics from computation plus a cross-data-domain persistent context - does not expire as LLMs and agents evolve or engine forms change.
  </details>

- **[A Discrete-Time Variational Objective for Degenerate Diffusion and Equivalence to Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00800)**  `arXiv:2611.00800`  
  _Rares Dolga, Harshad Dahake, David Barber_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion models and more recently Flow models have widespread application. In this work we consider degenerate Diffusion models in which the per-step generator is deterministic. We construct a modified variational framework and show a formal equivalence between Flow models and Degenerate Diffusion models. For our discrete-time variational objective we show that the optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of an infinite number of generator steps. Our work therefore provides a unified perspective, showing that discrete-time implementations of flow matching and the discrete-time Degenerate Diffusion model can be considered within the same simple variational framework, removing the need for the continuous-time machinery normally used to justify flow matching models.
  </details>

- **[BridgeDock: Taming Generative Co-Folding Prior for Molecular Docking with Diffusion Bridge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00795)**  `arXiv:2611.00795`  
  _Shikun Feng, Zipeng Yang, Qiuyi Li, Mingze Yin, Xiaoyuan Zhang, Tingjun Hou, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Molecular docking aims to predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex; in the conventional structure-based setting, it is conditioned on an input protein structure and ligand, often starting from an apo receptor in flexible docking or a holo receptor in rigid docking. Recent co-folding models exemplified by AlphaFold 3 achieve strong accuracy in protein-ligand complex prediction, but they typically generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and therefore do not directly use apo structures as structural priors in docking, leading to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings. We present BridgeDock, a framework that adapts pretrained co-folding backbones to flexible docking by modeling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, allowing generation from the initial protein-ligand state rather than from Gaussian noise. To make this bridge formulation compatible with pretrained denoisers, we introduce an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model. Experiments on standard flexible docking benchmarks show that BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines. Moreover, BridgeDock is computationally efficient at inference time and remains effective even with very few denoising steps.
  </details>

- **[One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00782)**  `arXiv:2611.00782`  
  _Jiaying Zhou, Jiachen Liu, Qingchao Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $\lambda$. The sign of $\lambda$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($\lambda{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($\lambda{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $\lambda{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.
  </details>

- **[Who Schedules Agent Memory? A Sidecar Approach to Long-Horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00779)**  `arXiv:2611.00779`  
  _Qijia Zhuang, Rui Liu, Yuxiang Ren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks, memory has become an important component for supporting sustained decision-making and action. Existing methods primarily focus on memory storage, updating, and retrieval, but often overlook how memory scheduling affects task execution: the main agent must identify memory needs, initiate retrieval, and wait for results while advancing the task, increasing both scheduling burden and execution time. To address this problem, we propose MemSidecar, which decouples memory scheduling from task execution through two independently selectable modes. Hooks directly delivers bound memory to the main agent when execution events match predefined conditions. Foresight uses an independent agent to predict potential queries, retrieve results in parallel, and store them in a cache, delivering matching and valid results when actual requests arrive. Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while effectively reducing execution costs and latency and improving the efficiency of long-horizon agent execution.
  </details>

- **[Decision-Centric Research: A Calibrated Decision Model and Benchmark for Scientific Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00774)**  `arXiv:2611.00774`  
  _Shaoning Zeng, Wen Huang, Xinzhong Zhu, Yi Duan, Jianhang Zhou, Jianping Gou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scientific agents make consequential choices about evidence, next actions and research strategy, but choices embedded in generated text are difficult to evaluate independently. Decision-Centric Research (DCR) is introduced to make individual choices the common unit of supervision, prediction and evaluation through typed predictions over an explicit Research State. DCR defines 24 decision types, ten of which are instantiated in the Research Decision Benchmark (RD-Bench) of 2,000 rule-generated cases. The Decision-Centric Research Model (DCRM) shares a candidate-token readout across types to produce answers and option probabilities in one forward pass. Under a held-out research-domain split, a 0.6B DCRM (state-aware) achieves 89.4% Top-1 accuracy, compared with 27.8% for DCRM (question-only) trained with the same recipe and 36.4% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. All 30 type-seed comparisons against DCRM (question-only) are significant after Holm correction. After held-out calibration, the resulting prediction sets contain a mean of 1.515 candidates at 97.1% empirical label coverage, reducing mean set size by 57.4% relative to DCRM (question-only) at similar coverage. These results establish a compact state-aware decision layer with accurate typed prediction and an inspectable uncertainty interface.
  </details>

- **[Designing Informative Actions: Action Construction for Long-Horizon Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00773)**  `arXiv:2611.00773`  
  _Alkut Arxidin, Shaoning Zeng, Jianhang Zhou, Jianping Gou, Xinzhong Zhu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language model agents support automated scientific research by connecting literature analysis and planning with experimentation. Evaluating which action an agent selects does not establish which experiment its instruction specifies, because omitted interventions or replication counts leave consequential choices to the executor. We introduce a reading-set framework for evaluating action construction under a common cost rule. Across 30 synthetic states, complete-design requests increase affordable efficiency by 465.98% and 327.91% relative to the action-name baseline in the two model families, respectively. An author-constructed research-action evaluation dataset provides 60 scenarios for complementary judgment evaluation. On this dataset, the scenario-level information-per-cost measure has a mean within-scenario correlation of 0.733 with judgments from 18 human participants. The framework makes design specification and execution ambiguity measurable, providing a reproducible basis for assessing how research agents translate scientific intent into informative, budget-feasible experiments.
  </details>

- **[Reading Between the Chapters: A Graph-Free RAG Rebuilt With AI and Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00752)**  `arXiv:2611.00752`  
  _Dipto Sumit, Syeda Fabiayee Jahan, Farig Sadeque_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Many questions about a book can only be answered by connecting passages chapters apart, such as a cough heard three times across a horse's life. We introduce CrossChapterQA, 1,853 such questions over 14 public-domain books. Each question lists the two to six chapters it needs (spanning half the book at the median) and the relation linking them, cites evidence from each, and has two independent reference answers graded blind. We use it to build LadderRAG, which indexes a book as passages, summaries and book-level cards for about $0.41 and answers a question for under a cent. Its first version failed mostly at retrieval. We redesigned it four times, steered by an LLM judge's verdicts and our analyses of failed answers: a design-level counterpart of RLAIF and RLHF in which feedback changes the architecture, not model weights. We also report the two redesigns that made answers worse. On the 191 questions its first version got wrong, the final version retrieves over twice as many required chapters on held-out books (recall 0.36 to 0.79), and ten annotators rate its answers 6.5/10 on average (764 ratings).
  </details>

- **[Inherited or Learned? Backdoor Selectivity in Distilled Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00748)**  `arXiv:2611.00748`  
  _Dipto Sumit, Sanzar Rahman, Ramisa Faria Puspita, Samiha Fairooz Urbi, Farig Sadeque_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Distillation is a routine step in building small language models, and a backdoored teacher can pass its backdoor to the student. We study what a student inherits when the backdoor is a rare string that triggers a fixed refusal. Keeping the trigger fixed, we vary only where it appears, at a random word boundary or appended to the instruction, and compare teachers and students on the exact trigger, six control strings and clean inputs. Across Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3, with 5% of transfer prompts triggered, randomly inserted triggers become less selective after distillation in all nine teacher-student pipelines, while appended triggers gain selectivity in Qwen and Llama and change little in Gemma. Students trained on the same prompts without a teacher show that much of this is not inherited. Llama and Gemma students learn an appended backdoor from the 150 poisoned examples alone, and only Qwen's 0.5B student needs the teacher. The data also sets where the trigger works. Gemma teachers respond to it anywhere, but their students only when it is appended. Audits should compare teacher and student on the same inputs, probe several trigger positions and include a student trained without the teacher.
  </details>

- **[Can Jev Improve Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Learning?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00737)**  `arXiv:2611.00737`  
  _Rui Song, Yingji Li, Hao Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Demonstration selection plays a crucial role in the effectiveness of in-context learning (ICL) for large language models (LLMs). Extensive research has explored various retrieval strategies to identify informative demonstrations and improve downstream performance. Recently, the emergence of Jev, a decision-oriented language model capable of producing probabilistic judgments, offers a new perspective on evaluating demonstration utility. This motivates us to investigate a fundamental question: Can Jev improve demonstration retrieval for in-context learning? In this paper, we demonstrate that Jev can effectively enhance demonstration retrieval by directly assessing the utility of candidate demonstrations for a given query. However, applying Jev to large-scale retrieval introduces substantial computational overhead, as each candidate requires an additional decision-making inference. To address this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective knowledge distillation approach that transfers Jev's utility estimation capability to a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP). By learning to approximate Jev's probabilistic judgments, the distilled model enables efficient demonstration ranking while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. Our study highlights the potential of decision-oriented language models for demonstration selection and provides an efficient framework for integrating their decision-making capabilities into ICL.
  </details>

- **[FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00645)**  `arXiv:2611.00645`  
  _Chen YanKai, Yu QiuHeng, Yuan Man, Zou Ting, Wu Lin, He Jian, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.
  </details>

- **[Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00633)**  `arXiv:2611.00633`  
  _YanKai Chen, Zhi Wan, ZiHao Li, Tao Jing_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,532 articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their steady-state reference efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.
  </details>

- **[TopoQuant: Topological Framework to Characterize Behavioral Shifts in Quantized Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00631)**  `arXiv:2611.00631`  
  _Baha Rababah, Shahzeb Qamar, Lorenz Sparrenberg, Rafet Sifa, Murat Kantarcioglu, Carson K. Leung, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.
  </details>

- **[Trail: Accurate Local Smart Home Control Using Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00610)**  `arXiv:2611.00610`  
  _Maleeha Masood, Deepak Vasisht, Indranil Gupta_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Natural-language driven smart home control remains challenging: cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) raise privacy concerns, while local Small Language Models (SLMs) can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests. We introduce Trail (Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes), a fully local framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions. Trail exploits the natural structure of a home's action space, selecting a room, device, and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry. This ensures valid actions while enabling confidence-based abstention when requests cannot be reliably resolved. We also design a structured memory module that uses typed decisions to support user preferences, device references, and multi-turn interactions. To evaluate Trail, we extend HomeBench and generate three datasets: Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variation; Trek-Robust, which evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description; and Trek-Memory, which assesses conversational memory across multi-turn interactions. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the requests that depend on earlier turns, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.
  </details>

- **[Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00602)**  `arXiv:2611.00602`  
  _Rocio Perales Valdes, Animesh Garg_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $\pi_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183,arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $\pi_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visitthis https URLfor video rollouts.
  </details>

- **[X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00596)**  `arXiv:2611.00596`  
  _XPeng, Boyang Wang, Boyi Sun, Chaoda Zheng, Dongbin Zhang, Guangfeng Jiang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents \emph{X-World~1.6}, advancing X-World~1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
  </details>

- **[State-Aware Activation Recomputation with Replay Contracts and Selective Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00590)**  `arXiv:2611.00590`  
  _Annan Zhang, Shengjie Song, Wenshuai Yao, Lihao Zhang, Tianmiao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Activation recomputation saves accelerator memory by replaying forward segments during the backward pass, but replay is only correct if it sees the state the original forward pass saw. Mutable buffers, aliased bytes and random-generator state can change in between, so re-executing unchanged code can differentiate a different computation. We make this state explicit. A versioned replay contract specifies what replay must restore, and a joint planner chooses, per segment, between activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots and selective-region preservation, charging each option its measured memory and recovery cost. Independent derivative and byte-level checks validate the contract, and a Torch/JAX cohort retains all 5,900 execution records, including matches, rejections and divergences. On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, each measured over fifty fresh processes, joint planning reduces paired step time by 18.16% against a correctly costed eager/whole planner at a 44 GiB budget (approximate 97.5% ratio interval $[.8172,.8195]$). At 32 GiB, where the eager/whole planner has no feasible static policy, joint planning is 4.98% faster than fixed regions at 29.94 rather than 26.20 GiB. A complete CIFAR-100 dense-queue application runs seven methods for 100 encoder and 25 probe epochs at six training seeds, with byte-identical test scores within each seed. There, joint planning uses 22.41% more allocated memory than whole snapshots, with a process-time geometric-mean ratio of 1.0080 (seed range $[.9845,1.0191]$). Together, the results map where selective preservation pays off: sparse writes with large activations benefit, while in the dense-queue workload whole snapshots use less allocated memory.
  </details>

- **[Evolving Scientific Intelligence: From Fragmented Evidence to Distributed Experimental Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00580)**  `arXiv:2611.00580`  
  _Yuheng Ding_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. We envision a different dynamic: in a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates evidence that stimulates further investigations. Such chains of information collision and empirical validation could transform isolated discovery loops into a cumulative scientific process. We propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint for enabling these evidence-driven chain reactions. ESI preserves experimental records in shared, computable scientific memory, where evidence from different domains can be recombined into testable hypotheses. It jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, then coordinates physical tests across distributed experimental nodes. Their feedback revises hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build the infrastructure for scientific intelligence that evolves through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.
  </details>

- **[WAR-CRAFT: Refining Web API Recommendations through Requirement Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00564)**  `arXiv:2611.00564`  
  _Zishuo Xu, Dezhong Yao, Zhiqiang Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Web API recommenders return a set of APIs for a mashup request but do not check it against provider documentation, the main public evidence of an API's capabilities. The set can therefore contain unsupported or redundant APIs and miss requested capabilities. Filling every apparent gap does not fix this, because a gap may already be served, may not need its own API, or may have no documented provider. We study post-recommendation refinement, which revises a frozen recommender's output using only the request, the catalog, and provider documentation. We propose WAR-CRAFT, which treats refinement as three decisions. An LLM removes unsupported or subsumed APIs by judging candidates jointly, then audits the remaining set against a requirement checklist derived from the request. For each uncovered requirement, a fine-tuned catalog-constrained Resolver proposes a catalog API or abstains, and an independent documentation check admits only supported proposals. On ProgrammableWeb with 7 heterogeneous upstream recommenders, WAR-CRAFT raises mean SetF1 from 0.558 to 0.644, above the strongest of 5 refinement baselines (62.5%), and roughly halves functional redundancy (0.127 to 0.065) without changing mean functional coverage. Gains range from +2.2 points on generative recommenders to +18.2 on fixed-cutoff rankers. At matched set sizes, WAR-CRAFT still outperforms truncating the upstream output, so the gain is not explained by set-size calibration alone. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Low-Margin Branch Points in Deterministic LLM Deliberatio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00546)**  `arXiv:2611.00546`  
  _Hajime Shimao, Warut Khern-am-nua_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deterministic multi-agent LLM deliberation can exactly re- play a fixed transcript, yet exact replay alone does not test local resistance to controlled internal interventions. Because each response becomes context for later agents, a changed greedy token can redirect a transcript-mediated execution. We present a white-box audit of this local failure mode in a five-agent committee under greedy decoding. We prospectively select low- and high-margin token positions, require exact no-op re- play, inject norm-relative residual displacements, and measure first transcript divergence within ten generated tokens. Low- margin positions are more branch-sensitive than high-margin controls, while matched margin-reducing gradient directions branch substantially more often than margin-increasing con- trols. We then continue selected realized branches through the committee to distinguish textual persistence from preference and final-decision changes. The contribution is a controlled audit for local branch susceptibility in this specified protocol, not an estimate of deployment frequency, decision correct- ness, or a phenomenon unique to multi-agent systems.
  </details>

- **[To Jev or Not to Jev: When Can System-1 Decision Models Replace LLM Judges?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00505)**  `arXiv:2611.00505`  
  _Shreyas Subramanian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer typed questions about a text (yes/no, multiple choice, or an ordinal score) with calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass and without generating text, which makes them an inexpensive candidate for LLM-as-a-judge workloads. We evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol, against four generative judges (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking) on eleven established judge benchmarks. Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and the two strongest, DReX-Max and d1-ultra, are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2. Conditioned on a reference answer generated once per prompt, eleven models reach 90.3-93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning, and on PPE best-of-16 every reference-guided System-1 judge matches GPT-5.6 with reasoning at roughly one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge and correlate more strongly with human helpfulness ratings. Robustness to instructions injected into the judged response is a property of the individual model rather than of the System-1 design: an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0-5% of the correct verdicts of five models but 17-49% for the other nine. Two general System-1 leaderboards that contain no judging tasks predict judging accuracy (Pearson r = 0.95-0.96), a well-calibrated System-1 first stage matches Opus on LLMBar while escalating 17% of items, and same-size controls show that the correctness deficit of a 4B decision model is a reasoning gap rather than a size gap.
  </details>

- **[Few Trials, Many Metrics: Beta Mixtures for Low-Budget AI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00474)**  `arXiv:2611.00474`  
  _Gustavo Tironi, Felipe Maia Polo, Diego Mesquita_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluating a stochastic AI system often requires many repeated samples per instance, especially for metrics defined over long horizons. Recent work has shown that modeling instance-level success probabilities with a Beta distribution recovers Pass@$k$ from far fewer samples than direct estimation. We show that this framework supports a broader range of evaluation targets. We fit a mixture of Beta distributions by marginal maximum likelihood, with the number of components chosen by BIC. From that one fit, we compute Pass$^k$ and AUC@$k$ at any horizon in closed form. We also derive delta-method confidence intervals for these metrics and for Pass@$k$, which require no additional model calls. Treating configurations rather than tasks as instances extends the same model to sensitivity analysis. For repeated success metrics, we find that mixture priors yield more accurate estimators than naive estimation across competition mathematics and graduate-level science benchmarks when extrapolating beyond the observed number of trials, and the resulting intervals cover the full-data reference. When prompts are treated as instances, it estimates the distribution of prompt sensitivity more accurately than a comparable item-response baseline without external covariates. Direct estimators remain preferable once trials reach the target horizon.
  </details>

- **[Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00464)**  `arXiv:2611.00464`  
  _Bhushit Nema, Siddharth Krishnamurthy, Anjali Kadiyala_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment viathis http URLconfirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.
  </details>

- **[Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00463)**  `arXiv:2611.00463`  
  _Alexander Krentsel, Sylvia Ratnasamy, Ion Stoica, Martin Casado, Ankur Goyal_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.
  </details>

- **[Nonconformal Distortion and Local Orientation Reversal in the Fourier Circuit of a Modular-Addition Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00414)**  `arXiv:2611.00414`  
  _Eduardo Fuentes, Gonzalo Riera, Héctor Allende-Cid_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We study the local differential geometry of a Fourier-based modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer whose algorithm has previously been reverse-engineered. For each of the five key Fourier frequencies, we restrict the model's multilayer perceptron (MLP) contribution to a corresponding Fourier input plane and readout, and measure its directional Beltrami coefficient under continuous input perturbations. Whereas nondegenerate restrictions of ideal complex multiplication are conformal, the trained maps exhibit nonconformal distortion (median $|\mu|=0.304$--$0.446$), spatial organization in the Beltrami argument, and regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies decreases from $0.939$ at initialization to $0.390$ after training. The key-frequency planes also show lower median distortion than most random-plane controls, although their distributions overlap and the coordinate frames differ in conditioning. Across 500 checkpoints in one training run, most of the aggregate reduction in Beltrami magnitude occurs before the principal increase in the measured Fourier-circuit formation. At the individual-input level, Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin ($|\rho|\leq0.026$). Late-checkpoint measurements across six runs show comparable distortion for most selected frequencies. These results provide a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified neural circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.
  </details>

- **[Hacking or Just Failing? A More Capable LLM Monitor Better Separates Reward Hacking from Honest Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00407)**  `arXiv:2611.00407`  
  _Kaushik Kezendirane_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  An agent's visible score can exceed its real progress because it gamed the score or because it simply made mistakes, so a useful reward-hacking monitor must tell the two apart. We built a sandboxed task in which an agent can game a completion score, labelled every episode by replaying it and repairing the final state counterfactually, and ran five pre-registered studies. On 60 episodes from a Llama 3.1 8B agent, small local monitors (Llama 3B and 8B) did not separate exploit attempts from honest failures with the same score gap: prompt changes traded missed exploits for false alarms, and the pre-registered primary monitor reached AUC 0.64. On identical inputs, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, which completed 9/10 clean tasks against 2/10 for the 8B model, met our pre-registered criterion (AUC 0.80, 95% interval [0.66, 0.93]; 1/35 honest failures flagged); with only 14 exploit episodes, this estimate is uncertain. On an exploit that no prompt names, Gemini usually described the action correctly yet never flagged it, in 5 and then 25 new episodes, even when manipulation was defined by its effect on the score. Given the full trace, the 8B monitor flagged all 25 replication episodes and none of 25 honest look-alikes, but its explanations described actions that had not occurred; given additional structured evidence, it also flagged 15 of the 25 look-alikes. A two-rule deterministic check caught every known exploit. We release the environment, labels, pre-registrations and per-judgement logs.
  </details>

- **[Dependence-Aware Risk Assessment and Optimal Design of AI-Agent Safeguard Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00386)**  `arXiv:2611.00386`  
  _Yijia Li, Maochao Xu, Peng Zhao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on safeguards to prevent unauthorized actions while preserving legitimate service. However, existing risk assessments often focus on individual safeguard performance while overlooking dependence among safeguard decisions. This paper develops a dependence-aware framework for risk assessment and optimal design of multi-component AI safeguard systems, jointly selecting configurations and operating policies for sequential layered screening and selective verification. We establish stochastic comparisons of layered-screening error probabilities and invocation costs under lower-orthant ordering. For selective verification, we characterize exactly which policies have error probabilities and review costs that respond monotonically to stronger dependence under supermodular ordering. For a fixed first stage and reviewer, we show that the optimal routing map is a two-threshold rule in the first-stage likelihood ratio. An accompanying open-source software package, Dependence-Aware Policy Optimization Algorithms (DAPOA), facilitates the practical implementation of the proposed framework. Numerical experiments show that ignoring dependence can lead to inaccurate risk assessments and infeasible safeguard designs, with independence-based selections violating security requirements in six of eight scenarios. An empirical study using four LLM safeguards on benchmark-derived agent actions further demonstrates the practical implications of dependence modeling. Under the principal operating setting, dependence-aware selection lowers held-out total cost by 39.6% relative to independence-based selection.
  </details>

- **[Efficient NPN Classification for Large Functions using Graph Neural Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00339)**  `arXiv:2611.00339`  
  _Chengdi Cao, Hanyu Wang, Wan-Hsuan Lin, Jason Cong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Two Boolean functions are considered NPN equivalent if one can be transformed into the other by negating inputs, permuting inputs, or negating the output. Efficient NPN classification is valuable in fields such as logic synthesis, quantum computing, and information theory. However, exact NPN classification demands exhaustive enumeration of all possible input permutations and negations. Its complexity grows exponentially, making it impractical for larger functions with more inputs. In this paper, we introduce the first learning-based formulation for NPN classification by recasting it as NPN action prediction. Our method represents Boolean functions as AND-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and applies a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network to predict input negations, output negation, and input permutations. To mitigate the non-canonicity of logic networks, we further introduce graph rewriting techniques that reduce structural ambiguity and recover useful symmetries before prediction. Experimental results show that NPN action prediction is learnable, that the resulting canonicalization quality improves over heuristic baselines, and that on practical benchmarks our method approaches exact methods on tractable cases while scaling to functions with up to 16 inputs.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00323)**  `arXiv:2611.00323`  
  _Zhuosheng Liu, Yihan Wu, Ziyun Xu, Xiaoxuan Liu, Longfei Yun, Kevin Han, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recommending creators that a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem: from hundreds of thousands of popular creators and only a short trail of prior engagements, the system must predict the next creator worth surfacing. The prevailing generative recommendation recipe tokenizes each creator into a \emph{Semantic ID} (SID) by quantizing a frozen embedding and trains a language model to generate SIDs. We show that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint. The creator-to-SID map is many-to-one, so colliding creators must be resolved by a popularity tie-break that caps creator-level recall and favors already-popular creators, and the frozen quantizer stops the training gradient from reaching the creator representation. We propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which gives every creator its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end. The map is bijective, so collisions are impossible and inference is a direct top-$k$ over creator logits. In a controlled comparison on production data in which the token layer is the only variable, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points ($1.84\times$) over a matched SID baseline, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged $64\times$, and serves at ${\sim}2.7\times$ lower per-user latency. The advantage carries over to the public KuaiRand dataset, where ACT is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline, provided each creator token sees enough training examples. In a live A/B test, ACT is directionally positive on every reported metric against both the SID-enhanced and the classic production rankers.
  </details>

- **[Quantifying Local and Global Fidelity of Nonlinear Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00290)**  `arXiv:2611.00290`  
  _Henry Han_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dimension reduction methods are chosen by a common claim: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local structure, and PCA preserves global structure. Checking it on given data takes local and global scores on one scale and a test that compares two maps. Both scores come from one curve. The locality profile is the chance-corrected share of each point's k nearest neighbors that a map keeps, over all neighborhood sizes. Its value at k = 10 is the local fidelity L, and its mean over 30 to 50 percent of the data is the global fidelity G. We prove that at the midpoint the profile is the agreement on which half of the data is near each point, a rank correlation of the distances. Because L and G are one statistic, two maps can be tested against each other. The LG reversal test applies to any two dimension reduction methods. It decides, with a block-jackknife p-value, whether one map is more local and the other more global, and returns the scale at which to change maps. On 156 maps of twelve datasets with up to 1.38 million points, G agrees with established global scores at 0.89 and 0.96, and 2,000 points estimate it. The test confirms the usual claim on seven datasets. On both retail datasets and both rolled-up manifolds, it finds the neighbor embeddings more global. In an agent memory of one million passages, the two maps cross at 150,000 passages (p = 2.6e-5). Applications span pathology, single cells, supply chains and AI agent memory.
  </details>

- **[Automated Theorem Generation in First-Order Logic by Construction from Triangular Standard Contradictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00269)**  `arXiv:2611.00269`  
  _Yang Xu, Shuwei Chen, Hailin Guo, Jun Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated theorem generation (ATG) seeks to construct new theorems rather than merely prove given conjectures. Existing approaches typically generate candidate statements that require subsequent proof or formal verification. We propose a constructive framework for ATG in first-order logic based on triangular standard contradictions. The method constructs minimally unsatisfiable clause sets from selected first-order literals, then forms theorems by retaining some clauses as premises and taking the negation of one clause, or a conjunction of clauses, as the conclusion. Minimal unsatisfiability ensures that the remaining premises are satisfiable, avoiding trivial inference by explosion, while unsatisfiability of the full set guarantees the resulting entailment. Theorems are therefore correct by construction, without a separate proof procedure for each instance. Extending the previously developed $\Delta_1$ generator, we introduce seven methods, $\Delta_2$--$\Delta_8$, forming a unified family of eight theorem-generation methods. Four generators, $\Delta_1$--$\Delta_4$, have been implemented and released. We also formulate a general $\Delta$-class method encompassing the family. Combinatorial analysis demonstrates the capacity to generate large numbers of distinct theorems systematically. This framework offers a principled foundation for automated theorem discovery and the construction of logically guaranteed knowledge.
  </details>

- **[A generative foundation model for computational brain imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00265)**  `arXiv:2611.00265`  
  _Yuting He, Xu Wen, Hongxing Lan, Chengliang Liu, Yuxing Liu, Yan Xi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.
  </details>

- **[Taurus: LLM-in-the-Loop CT Annotation Matches Coding Agents at Half the Cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00247)**  `arXiv:2611.00247`  
  _Bing Hu, Rishabh Sharma, Jatin Mehta_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dense labels of the aorta in CT are slow to draw, and the public aortic CT datasets that could stand in for them each label different structures under their own conventions. Large language model (LLM) agents can now write code and read images. We asked whether such a model labels these scans better as a free-form agent that writes its own segmentation code, or inside a harness, where an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. We built a harness, Taurus, and compared it with free-form agents by blind label recovery: we withheld the human labels of six public datasets (939 volumes) and scored every approach against each dataset's own classes. In the first version of Taurus, the model's review raised the primary metric on only two of six datasets, by less than the noise between two reviews of the same case. A free-form agent running Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher on most datasets. Moving what the free-form agents did well into the automated pass then carried most of the gain on 38 held-out cases. The final version smooths the label surfaces with a fixed rule and checks for the large errors the automated pass tends to make, such as an aneurysm drawn to half its size. Each check that fires puts a multiple-choice question to the model, with candidate corrections drawn on the scan. It matched the surface smoothness of the human references, and in the primary metric we found no difference from the free-form Opus agent, at under half its cost, $1.22 against $2.71 per case. Most of what made Taurus competitive came from the harness and its automation rather than from the language model itself. Taurus shows that this kind of annotation can be automated, so that expert time can move from drawing labels to checking them.
  </details>

- **[OmniPiano: Diverse Dexterous Piano-Playing Challenges for Standard, Robust, Safe, and Multi-Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00243)**  `arXiv:2611.00243`  
  _Fan Xu, Fan Yang, Yifan Xu, Ruiyuan Zhang, Yimou Wu, Nuo Yi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[RE-SciVQA: Improving Scientific VQA With Context-Relevant Retrieval and Lightweight MLLM Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00242)**  `arXiv:2611.00242`  
  _Sheikh Tahmim Mehdi, Muminul Islam Jami_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A deep understanding of scientific literature often relies on interpreting figures that contain key information beyond the main text. Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract insights from these figures can significantly accelerate knowledge discovery. Existing works on Scientific Visual Question Answering rely on resource-intensive training pipelines that are often inaccessible and require large computational resources. Instead of designing complex architectures, we propose RE- SciVQA, which focuses on improving the quality of retrieved context and fine-tuning small LLMs with parameter-efficient LoRA training. Using a simple query expansion step, relevant section headers are appended to the original question to improve the retrieval coverage. In addition, a simple adjustment of similarity scores is applied using figure references and caption alignment. On the SciVQA benchmark, RE-SciVQA achieves a ROUGE-1 F1 score of 73.9%, outperforming chart-focused models such as UniChart (14.7%), ChartGemma (6.9%), and Matcha-ChartQA (6.3%). Our relevance-enhanced RAG setup also improves the exact match by 11.9% and the fuzzy match by 29.5% compared with a standard RAG baseline, resulting in an overall gain of 14.3%. We also examine closed-ended infinite visual questions, a category in which chart-understanding models often struggle. Our experiments show that using plot digitization instead of synthetic captions leads to an 18.5% improvement for this question type.
  </details>

- **[From Cross-Section to Cross-Omics: Conditional Cell Nucleus Image Editing in Spatial Transcriptomics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00226)**  `arXiv:2611.00226`  
  _Yuechen Yang, Junchao Zhu, Junlin Guo, Yanfan Zhu, Ruining Deng, Zhengyi Lu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) platforms simultaneously measure gene expression and capture cell nucleus images at single-cell resolution. A fundamental property of tissue preparation introduces a confounding relationship between the two measurement modalities: sectioning a three-dimensional tissue into a thin slice produces a two-dimensional cross-section whose area depends on the cutting angle.
