- **[Déjà Vu: Cycle-Consistent Re-ranking for Semantic Correspondence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00328)**  `arXiv:2611.00328`  
  _Xiaoran Zhang, Huidong Liu, Yang Liu, Chien-Chih Wang, Jinfa Huang, Lingkai Kong, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We propose \emph{Déjà Vu}, a test-time decoding module for semantic correspondence. Matching semantically equivalent keypoints across images of the same object category is challenging due to variations in appearance, viewpoint, and scale. While features from large pretrained vision models carry strong zero-shot correspondence ability, existing methods reduce final matching to greedy top-$1$ nearest-neighbor selection. We show that the correct correspondence appears among the top-ranked candidates far more often than top-$1$ matching achieves: with $30$ candidates, zero-shot features exceed the top-$1$ accuracy of a supervised model. This reveals a \textit{decoding bottleneck} rather than a limit of the representation. Motivated by this observation, we formulate semantic correspondence as a \textit{recall-then-rerank} problem. Our method first nominates an adaptive candidate set, larger when the similarity distribution is ambiguous and smaller when it is confident, then re-ranks the candidates with a graded cycle-consistency score: each candidate is matched back to the source image and penalized by how far its reverse match lands from the original keypoint. The module operates entirely on the similarity matrix already computed by the base method. It consistently improves three representative baselines on SPair-71k, its geometric subset, and PF-Pascal under both unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, with gains of up to $+1.8$ PCK@0.10 on SPair-71k and $+3.4$ PCK@0.15 on PF-Pascal, and $+4.9$ under Keypoint Average Precision.
  </details>

- **[Seeing the Unseen: Unified Visible--Invisible Motion for Physically Consistent Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00293)**  `arXiv:2611.00293`  
  _Mingyang Bao, Fangda Ye, Xihao Chen, Bobo Li, Jason Li, Shengqiong Wu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in video generation have achieved impressive visual quality, yet they often fail to produce physically consistent dynamics due to the lack of explicit modeling of underlying physical processes. Existing approaches either rely on simulators with strong assumptions or use coarse semantic guidance, and further struggle to effectively inject physical priors into generation models. In this work, we propose Seeing the Unseen, a unified framework for physics-grounded video generation. Our approach decomposes the problem into two stages: learning physical dynamics and injecting them into video synthesis. First, we introduce a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS) that learns generalizable physical interactions from data and predicts plausible 3D motion trajectories. Second, we propose a Visible--Invisible Motion Field (VIMF) that captures both motion observable in the input frame and motion that emerges over time due to object dynamics. This representation enables more complete and structured motion guidance compared to conventional physical signals. By integrating these trajectories into a diffusion-based generator, our method produces videos that are both visually coherent and physically consistent. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and reduced physical artifacts compared to strong baselines.
  </details>

- **[Seeing Less in a Sparse World: Cross-View Geolocalization from Limited Field-of-View Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00288)**  `arXiv:2611.00288`  
  _Fahimul Aleem, Shruti Vyas_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cross-view geolocalization aims to determine the geographic location of a ground-level image by retrieving its corresponding satellite image, offering a promising alternative for localization in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied or degraded environments such as urban canyons, dense forests, and disaster scenarios. Despite recent progress, existing approaches remain limited by the lack of globally diverse training datasets and benchmarks that are often geographically restricted. Furthermore, most benchmarks rely on panoramic ground views, which do not reflect the limited field-of-view imagery captured by real world cameras.To address these challenges, we introduce Cross-View World 500k (CVW500k), a large-scale globally distributed dataset containing over 500,000 ground-satellite image pairs collected across diverse geographic regions and environments. Unlike previous datasets, CVW500k uses limited field-of-view ground images, providing a more realistic and challenging setting for cross-view geolocalization. In addition, we propose GeoQueryNet, a query-based cross-view fusion transformer framework designed to bridge the viewpoint gap between ground and satellite images. The model leverages a CLIP-based visual encoder with parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation and introduces a Cross-View Alignment Module that uses learnable query tokens to extract geographically consistent features across viewpoints. Our code can be found here:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[SketchForge: Training-Free Scene-to-Vector Sketching via Decoupled Structure and Texture Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00253)**  `arXiv:2611.00253`  
  _Quang-Thinh Nguyen, Duy-Khang Do, Hien Trinh, Tam V. Nguyen, Minh-Triet Tran, Trung-Nghia Le_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Converting a raster image into a resolution-independent, stroke-editable vector sketch while faithfully preserving both structural contours and tonal texture remains challenging: raster-space rendering pipelines are difficult to edit at the stroke level, while generation-from-scratch vectorization methods struggle to remain faithful to an arbitrary input image. We present SketchForge, a training-free framework that converts an input raster image into a resolution-independent SVG sketch through per-instance test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. Strokes are seeded via a contour and attention-guided initialization, then refined by a vector-native differentiable rendering pipeline that decouples structural contour strokes from free-form texture strokes under dedicated objectives, composited via multiply-blend layering. Extensive experiments show that SketchForge consistently outperforms existing vector-based baselines in structural fidelity and generation quality. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[SketchBloom: Training-Free Vector Sketch Outpainting with Stroke-Level Style Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00245)**  `arXiv:2611.00245`  
  _Quang-Thinh Nguyen, Duy-Khang Do, Tam V. Nguyen, Minh-Triet Tran, Trung-Nghia Le_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Outpainting sparse sketches while preserving contour coherence and stroke style remains challenging. We present SketchBloom, a training-free framework that combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization. Given a sketch, a scene prompt, and an optional reference style, it produces an editable Scalable Vector Graphic (SVG) composed of Bezier strokes. Adaptive latent blending balances content contours and reference texture without model retraining. A reference-derived stroke vocabulary initializes contour- and DINO-attention-guided strokes, which are optimized separately for structure and texture before contour-emphasizing multiply fusion. As in prior optimization-based vector sketching, no task-specific network is trained; our contribution is the synthesis design specialized to sketch outpainting. On LineArtOut-1K, comprising 1,024 input and style combinations, SketchBloom improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over the evaluated vector baselines when all methods vectorize the same outpainted raster. This protocol evaluates vector synthesis rather than end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority. Runtime is approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[CDBM: Complexity-Diversity Framework for Building Morphology Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00122)**  `arXiv:2611.00122`  
  _Evgenii Maslov, Alexandra Vabnits, Denis Karpov, Alexey Morozov, Anastasia Antsiferova, Art Prosvetov, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce Complexity-Diversity Building Metrics (CDBM), twelve interpretable descriptors for building massings represented as vertical extrusions. They measure how strongly geometric detail is expressed (complexity) and how unevenly it varies across one- and two-dimensional elements (diversity). Computed for 482,241,306 OpenStreetMap buildings and compared with 3D Building Metrics (3DBM) and the LION shape latent on task-specific samples, CDBM is tested on function, region, contextual relevance, real-generated discrimination, human preference and geometry-conditioned generation. With gradient boosting, CDBM best separates generated from mapped massings and best matches human preference; with logistic regression it matches 3DBM on realism. 3DBM leads on the other three tasks. As generation targets, the descriptors show that models struggle to produce strongly expressed and heterogeneous forms. CDBM complements existing indicators.
  </details>

- **[DTP-OPSD: Reinforcement Learning with Distractor-Aware Temporal-Privilege On-Policy Self-Distillation for Temporal Video Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00120)**  `arXiv:2611.00120`  
  _Zhaoyu Chen, Yongwei Nie_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Temporal Video Grounding (TVG) aims to localize the start and end times of an event described by a language query in a video. The task becomes particularly challenging when the same video contains multiple repeated, similar, or opposite events. On these hard examples, all responses sampled by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) may miss the target and receive zero temporal Intersection-over-Union (tIoU). Their group-relative advantages are then all zero, leaving no useful policy gradient signal. To address this, we propose DTP-OPSD, a reinforcement learning framework with distractor-aware temporal-privilege on-policy self-distillation. The student observes the clean video and generates responses on-policy, while a shared-weight teacher observes a privileged video in which the target window is marked by red full-frame borders and same-video distractor windows by blue full-frame borders. For the distillation loss, the teacher evaluates student-generated prefixes and provides dense token-level Jensen-Shannon divergence supervision. This supervision remains informative even when GRPO provides no policy gradient signal. We suppress distillation when the teacher does not outperform the student and strengthen it for groups where the teacher performs better but all student rollouts receive zero tIoU. We also construct a compact hard-interference training set through VLM screening and human verification. With only 300 additional post-training examples, DTP-OPSD achieves the highest mIoU among the compared open-source 8B models on Charades-TimeLens, ActivityNet-TimeLens, and QVHighlights-TimeLens, reaching 55.93, 54.77, and 66.71, respectively. Compared with Pure GRPO trained on the same data, DTP-OPSD improves all 12 reported metrics, with R1@0.7 gains of 1.28, 1.62, and 1.78 points on the three benchmarks. Code will be released atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Brain-Behavior Modeling from Multimodal MRI using Opportunistic Pretraining and Common-Cohort Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00114)**  `arXiv:2611.00114`  
  _Md. Tanvir Rahman, Taslima Ferdaus Shuva, Nabil Anan Orka, Asaduzzaman Khan, Mohammad Ali Moni_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Incomplete imaging coverage limits sample sizes for multimodal cognitive prediction. We evaluated a two-stage opportunistic deep ensemble using baseline Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study data to predict fluid, crystallized, and total cognition. Separate neural models processed structural/diffusion, resting-state, and task-based MRI data with covariates. Models were pretrained on eligible modality cohorts (up to 9,686 participants), adapted to common training cohorts, and fused via Ridge regression (trimodal cohort: 4,216 participants). Five-fold family-aware cross-validation compared this approach against constituent and covariate-only models. Two-stage training increased mean test coefficient of determination (R^2) in 24 of 27 comparisons (median gain: 0.0081). Fusion increased mean R^2 by 0.0051-0.0333 over the strongest constituent and reduced mean absolute error by 0.0067-0.0976. Task-plus-resting-state and trimodal ensembles reduced absolute error across all targets (nominal p <= 0.0108). Task-plus-resting-state fusion achieved the highest mean R^2 for fluid (0.2222) and total cognition (0.3665), while structural-plus-resting-state led for crystallized cognition (0.3706), yielding R^2 gains of 0.0805, 0.1180, and 0.0890 over covariate-only references. Ablations showed expanded pretraining drove most improvements. Gradient-based attribution identified target-dependent input patterns. These findings support using partially observed cohorts for model development to achieve modest fusion gains. Pending external validation, this approach may support MRI-informed cognitive phenotyping.
  </details>

- **[Predicting Cognitive Profiles from Structural MRI using Spatial Graph Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00113)**  `arXiv:2611.00113`  
  _Taslima Ferdaus Shuva, Md. Tanvir Rahman, Risala Tasin Khan, Mohammad Ali Moni, ASM Ashraf Mahmud_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Predicting cognitive abilities from structural neuroimaging remains challenging due to the high dimensionality and geometric complexity of brain morphology. Conventional models typically flatten regional morphometry into tabular features, failing to explicitly represent spatial relationships. We propose a Spatial-Topological Graph Neural Network (ST-GNN) to predict four distinct cognitive phenotypes across large pediatric cohorts (N = 2,378 to 2,424). By projecting regional morphometry onto a population-level standardized spatial graph, ST-GNN restricts message passing to defined neighboring regions. Evaluations demonstrate that ST-GNN effectively fuses spatial morphology with systemic covariates, outperforming linear baselines and topology-free deep models. Ablations reveal that imposing a sparse geometric topology (K-nearest neighbors) and utilizing global feature scaling - which preserves absolute morphometric scale - outperform fully connected networks and region-normalized approaches. These choices provide transferable architectural inductive biases, revealing differences between computational routing and morphometric feature attribution. Integrated Gradients analysis identified distinct morphological features consistent with neuroanatomical evidence, such as cerebellar volume for working memory and superior frontal surface area for executive function. These findings suggest standardized structural MRI provides useful information for task-specific cognitive prediction, establishing a foundation for MRI-based neurodevelopmental assessment.
  </details>

- **[Dynamic Merging Mutually-Distilled Multi-View Networks for RGB-Event-based Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00107)**  `arXiv:2611.00107`  
  _Futian Wang, Fan Zhang, Xiao Wang, Yuhe Ding, Shiao Wang, Jingxi Huang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-modal fusion algorithms combining conventional frame-based cameras and event cameras have recently attracted substantial research attention. Typically, existing approaches convert event streams into frames, voxels, or tensors, and then learn the required spatiotemporal information from these transformed event representations for fusion with conventional frame-camera data. Obviously, such paradigms only exploit the limited representational capacity of event data. Moreover, standard training pipelines fail to fully leverage diverse model parameters obtained throughout the learning process. In this paper, we propose a novel mutual distillation method leveraging multi-view teacher network weights to better integrate multiple event representations and achieve model-parameter level fusion. Specifically, we employ multiple encoders to extract different types of event representations and perform mutual knowledge distillation at both the feature-level and logit-level in this process. Afterwards, we perform a dynamic hierarchical model merge strategy on the model parameters from the first stage to yield a unified multi-modal RGB-Event representation model. Experimental results across multiple event-based datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves significant performance improvements.
  </details>

- **[A Novel Lightweight Multi-Scale Branching Encoder for Few-Shot Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00099)**  `arXiv:2611.00099`  
  _Oriod Malo, Alexandre Xavier Falcão, Laurent Najman_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Few-Shot Learning (FSL) addresses classification scenarios in which only a small number of labeled examples are available for each class. This paper presents the Sum12 Multi-Scale branching encoder, a lightweight convolutional architecture designed to improve the embedding stage of Prototypical Networks without substantially increasing computational cost. The encoder uses seven parallel convolutional branches whose kernel-size combinations sum to 12, allowing local and broader spatial structures to be represented within a unified Multi-Scale feature space. The proposed architecture was evaluated on Omniglot, CIFAR- FS, FC100, and miniImageNet under controlled few-shot learning protocols and compared with the original Prototypical Network encoder and Inception-inspired branch variants. Additional ablation studies have investigated fusion strategies, dilated convolutions, branch compositions, and receptive field budget. Beyond few-shot learning, the encoder was also tested on the MedMNIST 2D benchmark to assess its behavior in conventional supervised medical image classification. Across these experiments, Sum12 generally improved the low-shot classification performance with respect to the basic ProtoNet encoder while preserving a compact model size. These properties suggest that the proposed encoder may be suitable for low-data visual recognition and resource-constrained intelligent imaging applications. However, complete end-to- end validation on the target embedded platform, including resolution of the observed implementation discrepancies, remains future work.
  </details>

- **[Pano2BIM: A Geometry-Constrained Vision-Language Agent for As-Built BIM Generation from a Floor Plan and a Single 360$^\circ$ Image](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00097)**  `arXiv:2611.00097`  
  _Juan Diego Castaño Molina, Borja García de Soto_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Digital twins require accurate, up-to-date building information models (BIM) that reflect physical conditions, yet generating and maintaining as-built models remains costly and labor-intensive. Emerging image-based methods can capture visual appearance without inherently producing structured BIM information, while vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with reliable metric object placement. This paper presents Pano2BIM, a geometry-constrained VLM agent that generates approximate IFC4 models at Level of Development (LOD) 200 from a floor plan with known room dimensions and a single 360-degree photograph. The VLM identifies landmarks and objects, while deterministic tools estimate camera pose, compute metric positions through ray casting, and check spatial constraints. An optional second stage enriches the presentation model through render-and-compare feedback without modifying the primary furniture geometry. In a preliminary evaluation on one laboratory, the proposed Measure workflow achieved a mean furniture-footprint intersection over union (IoU) of 0.53, compared with 0.44 for a single-response baseline using identical modeling instructions, and matched an average of 4.0 versus 2.3 of seven fixed furniture elements across three runs. Centroid disagreements were similar for the four elements consistently identified by both approaches. The measurement stage averaged 3.8 minutes and USD 1.63 in API costs per run, while the complete demonstrated workflow required approximately 42 minutes and USD 11. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of rapid, low-cost as-built BIM generation, with potential applications in maintaining digital twins that reflect changing physical conditions.
  </details>

- **[OCRia-1 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00092)**  `arXiv:2611.00092`  
  _Aman Rangapur, Antonio Jimeno Yepes, Daniel Bustamante, Nutchapol Dendumrongsup, Sebastián G. Acosta, Pierre-Loïc Doulcet, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce OCRia-1, a 4B vision-language model (VLM) for document parsing that excels at preserving table structure, extracting chart data and retaining text formatting. OCRia-1 handles content that has traditionally been challenging in document parsing: merged cells and spanning headers, tables with thousands of cells, chart data, and meaningful text formatting such as bold, italics, subscripts and superscripts, preserving details needed for business-critical document analysis. At the time of this report, it achieves the highest scores on tables, charts and text formatting among the systems evaluated, including a 35B model and Mistral OCR 4.1. Its mean ParseBench score over the four dimensions we evaluate is 0.87, against 0.75 for the next-best system.We emphasize data quality and reward design in training OCRia-1. Synthetic pages provide exact ground truth for long tables and rich formatting, while real pages are transcribed using a pipeline grounded in the PDF text layer. We attribute OCRia-1's performance primarily to careful data curation that prioritizes quality and diversity over quantity. Dimension-specific rewards evaluate table reconstruction, chart-data extraction and text-formatting fidelity. We train the model on the curated data using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then refine it through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).To our knowledge, OCRia-1 is the fastest published document-parsing VLM in its class, decoding at about 4,700 tokens per second with a single request on one B200 GPU, about nine times faster than the base model on stock vLLM. This is achieved through a block-diffusion speculator, quantization and custom kernels.
  </details>

- **[Rethinking Feature Perturbation for Single-Source Domain Generalization: A Representation-Space Analysis and Spectral Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00091)**  `arXiv:2611.00091`  
  _Badr-Eddine Benelmostafa, Sohaib Baroud_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Feature perturbation is widely used in single-source domain generalization (SSDG), yet it is typically evaluated by task performance rather than by the representation changes it induces. We investigate whether perturbations can be compared through measurable descriptors of these changes. We introduce a four-dimensional representation-space description comprising feature displacement $D_F$, relational displacement $D_R$, a task-region ratio $\Theta_{\mathrm{Task}}$, and subspace deviation $\Theta_{\mathrm{Subspace}}$. We use these descriptors as an empirical analysis framework, not as a universal geometry, to characterize existing perturbation mechanisms. Across two object-detection settings involving style and weather shifts, we observe distinct geometric profiles and a concentration of relatively strong out-of-domain (OOD) configurations within a bounded region of the descriptor space. These findings do not establish a universal optimum but motivate investigating whether regions associated with stronger SSDG performance can be identified without target-domain access. As a case study, we introduce Dual-Invariant Spectral Perturbation (DISP), a non-learned Fourier-phase perturbation with explicit controls over phase magnitude $\rho$, channel coupling $\kappa$, and frequency support $\mathcal{M}$. We empirically examine how these controls affect the proposed descriptors. DISP achieves strong OOD performance in our experiments, illustrating how explicit perturbation controls can be analyzed through a representation-space description. We hope this viewpoint can contribute to more interpretable, controllable, and ultimately testable approaches to feature perturbation in SSDG.
  </details>

- **[AdaptAD: Foundation Model Adaptation with Missing Modality Robustness for Alzheimer's Disease Staging Across the Disease Continuum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00084)**  `arXiv:2611.00084`  
  _Dawa Chyophel Lepcha, Sophie A. Martin, Pierrick Coupé, Shabbir Syed Abdul_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Staging Alzheimer's disease (AD) across its continuum, from cognitively normal (CN) through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia from a single structural MRI remains difficult because 3-D networks overfit small cohorts, and FreeSurfer morphometry is often unavailable. We present AdaptAD, which reads a registered T1-weighted scan as 16 anatomically placed 2.5-D slices through the medial temporal lobe and adapts a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), training 3.5 M of 89 M parameters. Morphometry enters as tokens when present, or as a learned [MISSING] token, and a missing-aware stacker fuses both experts. Under a pre-registered protocol, ten methods were compared for three-class CN/MCI/AD staging on identical 5-fold splits of 597 ADNI participants, 29% without FreeSurfer, with Holm-corrected paired bootstrap tests. The locked model was tested once on 993 OASIS-3 participants (988 scored by every method). On ADNI, AdaptAD achieved a three-class macro-AUC of 0.745 (95% CI 0.709 to 0.781), ranking first and significantly exceeding full fine-tuning, ShaSpec and a 3-D CNN. On OASIS-3 it reached 0.780 (0.748 to 0.814), and on the CDR-based label (0.804) it significantly outperformed every 3-D and image-tabular method. LoRA matched full fine-tuning with 25 times fewer trainable parameters, and removing morphometry changed external macro-AUC by less than 0.003. The disease score tracked MMSE and CDR-SB within diagnostic groups and stratified MCI-to-dementia progression (log-rank p < 0.001), while saliency concentrated in medial temporal and periventricular regions. A parameter-efficient 2-D foundation model can therefore stage the full AD continuum from a routine T1 scan without morphometry, offering a scalable route to memory-clinic deployment.
  </details>

- **[Sequential Transfer Learning for Plant Disease Recognition Across Perennial Crop Domains Using MobileNetV2-CBAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00080)**  `arXiv:2611.00080`  
  _Ropkathaa Choudhury_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Purpose: This study investigates whether a learned disease-recognition representation can be progressively reused across distinct perennial crop domains and how its predictive behaviour changes as target-domain heterogeneity increases.Design/methodology/approach: A lightweight MobileNetV2 framework enhanced with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) was evaluated through sequential transfer from Walnut to Cashew, Coffee and Mango, followed by validation on the heterogeneous ABCGMP six-crop benchmark. Each stage used the preceding model representation and was evaluated on an independent test set using complementary classification measures.Findings: Test accuracy increased from 75.76% for the Walnut baseline to 84.85% after CBAM integration, followed by 90.67% on Cashew, 100.00% on Coffee and 99.50% on Mango. The final ABCGMP evaluation achieved 88.44% accuracy, 81.49% Balanced Accuracy and 0.9949 ROC-AUC. The results show that substantial predictive capability was retained through successive crop transfers, while broader multi-crop heterogeneity introduced a measurable performance constraint.Originality: The study provides an empirical characterisation of sequential knowledge reuse across multiple perennial crop domains using a common lightweight attention-enhanced representation, extending evaluation beyond isolated source-to-target transfer.
  </details>

- **[Faithful Where You Look: Anchor-Based Evaluation Hides Text Fabrication in Image-Conditioned Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00079)**  `arXiv:2611.00079`  
  _Yujia Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Image-conditioned video models are used to show real places, so whether their output stays faithful to the place they were shown is a practical question. The text benchmarks we found that check fidelity against a reference do so at an anchor - an annotated region, typically the sign the task is about. We show that this choice hides most of the failure. We conditioned four models from three vendors on 48 street-level references of Tokyo storefronts and measured text fidelity at the annotated sign and in the periphery, the other text the reference covers. At the anchor, all four models are close to a no-model control (anchor text fidelity 0.90-0.94 against 0.996) and are not reliably separated from one another. In the periphery, 36-54% of generated text regions have no counterpart in the reference, against 1.6% for the control, although every prompt forbade new readable text. Two blinded raters agree on which regions are fabricated (kappa = 0.83-0.96), the result held in preregistered rounds on two vendors whose videos the measure had never seen (42% and 56%), and VBench-I2V's reference-based consistency scores show no evidence of tracking it in our sample. Most fabricated text is legible-looking text where the reference shows none or cannot be read - a form that string-matching metrics discard, which is why our own first measure missed it. A preregistered Latin-script replication in London missed its bar in a first round and met it in an independent second round. We release code, annotations, per-video scores, ratings and every preregistration. Code and data:this https URL
  </details>

- **[AegisBench: Auditing Aerial Search-and-Rescue Person Detection Under the Conditions It Is Deployed In](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00077)**  `arXiv:2611.00077`  
  _Amogh Vinaykumar, Prem Kamasani_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Drone-based person detection is being adopted by emergency-management agencies to find missing people faster than ground teams can. The benchmarks behind that adoption were collected in calm, clear daylight, while the missions that trigger deployment happen in floods, wildfires, storms, and at night. AegisBench measures that gap. It applies nine physically motivated corruptions from four disaster families, each at three severities monotone in a declared image statistic or physical quantity, to two aerial search-and-rescue datasets, HERIDAL and SARD. Three architecturally distinct detectors (Faster R-CNN, YOLOv11, RT-DETR) are scored across 168 conditions by one shared evaluator, at confidence thresholds frozen on clean validation data as a fielded system would run. Robustness is highly uneven. Low light is the extreme case: a 4.5-stop exposure loss drives recall to exactly zero for all three detectors on both datasets, a result that holds under threshold-free mAP and across three training seeds, and is mirrored on 300 real night drone images, where 2 of 759 people are found. Surviving detections largely stay on target, so the failure is silent: an empty frame looks the same as one whose occupants the system cannot see. Fine-tuning on milder low-light levels recovers 0.06 to 0.19 recall at the held-out severity, at an architecture-dependent cost on other conditions, and does not transfer to real night imagery. Spatial corruptions rank differently on the two datasets, which we cannot attribute to altitude alone because their parameters scale with frame size rather than person size. We release the corruption engine, evaluation pipeline, and all per-condition results as an audit instrument for anyone evaluating these systems.
  </details>

- **[When Morphs Look Better: Face Image Quality as a Training-Free Signal for Morphing Attack Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00074)**  `arXiv:2611.00074`  
  _Hao Peng, Fu Bo, Mahmoud Elshirbeny, Guray Ozgur_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Face image quality assessment (FIQA) estimates the utility of a face image for automated face recognition and has been proposed as a morphing attack detection (MAD) signal that requires no morph-specific training. We evaluate 17 FIQA methods from all current FIQA categories on 20 morphing attack sets from two datasets, FRLL and FEI, including five diffusion-based attack sets. Each quality score is used directly as a MAD decision score. Unlike prior work, which inverted a quality measure when this lowered its error, we fix the score direction of each method in advance from its definition, so that cases in which morphs receive higher quality than bona fide samples remain visible. On FRLL, DifFIQA(R) achieves a mean D-EER of 11.42%, and together with CLIB-FIQA and eDifFIQA(L) clearly outperforms all other FIQA methods. A strong separation of bona fide and morph scores does not imply good detection performance: on the diffusion-based attacks, up to 11 of 17 methods assign higher quality to morphs than to bona fide samples, and the largest reversed separation in the study coincides with the worst detection result of the study. Performance also depends strongly on the attack: GraFIQs(L), the best detector of DCMorph and Arc2Morph on FRLL, performs poorly on the landmark-based and GAN-based attacks. On FEI, the lowest mean D-EER is 39.75%, and a threshold set on the bona fide data of one dataset does not transfer to the other.
  </details>

- **[CRaFT-XDet: Causal and Robust Fusion Transformer for Dual-Energy X-ray Prohibited Item Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00072)**  `arXiv:2611.00072`  
  _Moinul Hossain, Munshaibur Rahman Mahin, Taskin Khaleque, Mohammad Sakib Mahmood, M. F. Mridha, Md. Jakir Hossen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated prohibited item detection in X-ray security imagery is fundamentally constrained by severe object overlap, scanner-dependent domain shifts, and spurious correlations induced by cluttered baggage composition. Existing detectors largely rely on appearance-driven supervision, limiting their robustness and cross-scanner generalisation. We introduce CRaFT-XDet, a causality-grounded and physics- motivated detection framework that reformulates X-ray threat detection as invariant representation learning under attenuation-driven modality variation. Our approach is grounded in a Scanner-Invariant Causal Detection formalisation (Theorem 1), which establishes that minimising the proposed Causal Invariance Regularisation (CIR) objective across partitioned scanner environments approximates the interventional distribution P (Y | do(Xobj)) under standard identifiability assumptions, providing a principled causal formulation for dual-energy X-ray detection. CRaFT-XDet integrates: (i) causal feature disentanglement to suppress context-induced shortcuts; (ii) physics-motivated regularisation to enforce material-consistent embeddings; and (iii) transformer-based cross-energy interaction modelling for structured reasoning in cluttered scenes. With 29.2 M parameters, 89.5 GFLOPs, and 345 FPS (1.7 ms inference), CRaFT-XDet is real-time deployable. Trained on SIXray with five-fold cross-validation, the framework achieves 0.9389 mAP@0.5 and 0.8021 mAP@0.5:0.95. Without domain adaptation, CRaFT-XDet maintains strong cross- dataset performance on OPIXray and HiXray, indicating robust generalization across heterogeneous scanner distributions. In category-agnostic binary threat detection, the model attains 93.92% recall and 0.9031 mean IoU, highlighting reliability in safety-critical screening where missed detections are costly.
  </details>

- **[How Reliable Are Object Detection Models Beyond Clear Weather? A Deployment-Oriented Robustness Study for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00071)**  `arXiv:2611.00071`  
  _Munshaibur Rahman Mahin, Isha Das, Most. Sonia Islam, Mohammad Sakib Mahmood, M. F. Mridha, Md. Jakir Hossen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autonomous driving perception systems must maintain reliable object detection under diverse environmental conditions, not only in clear daytime scenes. However, the cross-weather robustness of modern detectors remains insufficiently characterised under source-only evaluation. This study evaluates representative object detection architectures trained exclusively on clear daytime driving scenes and tested without adaptation under unseen fog, rain, snow, and night conditions. The evaluation covers lightweight and medium-scale one-stage, two-stage, and transformer-based detectors within a unified protocol. Robustness is assessed using performance Drop (%), a Weather Robustness Index (WRI), and class-level sensitivity analysis for critical road participants, including cars, buses, trucks, and persons. Prediction confidence reliability under environmental domain shift is measured using Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Results reveal consistent performance degradation in adverse conditions, reaching 62.90% at night. Buses show the highest sensitivity to environmental variability, while cars remain comparatively stable across weather transitions. Comparisons indicate that YOLO-based detectors exhibit the lowest calibration mismatch, reflecting stronger agreement between predicted confidence and empirical detection correctness. In contrast, DETR achieves the lowest robustness score, with a WRI of 0.6859, indicating greater vulnerability to cross-weather domain shift. These findings offer deployment-oriented insights into detector robustness and confidence reliability for safety-critical intelligent vehicle perception systems.
  </details>

- **[MedICL: Modality-Anatomy-Aware Visual In-Context Learning for Medical Visual Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00067)**  `arXiv:2611.00067`  
  _Ji-jun Park, Soo-joon Choi, Seungmin Han, Haeun Kwon, Jiwon Jeong, Taeyang Yoon_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Training-free adaptation of medical vision-language models (LVLMs) is a deployment requirement, yet visual in-context learning (ICL) injects modality- and style-mismatched demonstrations into medical contexts, teaching a frozen model the wrong answering style. We present MedICL, which curates demonstrations instead of retraining the model. MADS selects modality-anatomy aligned demonstrations that cover complementary interpretation dimensions; W2C curates them with weak retrieval signals and a strong verification vote that checks demonstrations rather than the model's own outputs; ECC answers with W anchored demonstration sets, aggregates by abnormality-aware signatures, and re-answers once on conflict. On VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA under the LLaVA-Med zero-shot protocol, MedICL improves the strongest zero-shot baseline by +11 - +14 points on open-ended and +7 - +14 on closed questions, recovers 71% of fine-tuned open-ended performance on VQA-RAD at zero training cost, and stays robust to shifted or corrupted demonstration banks.
  </details>

- **[Comparing Monocular and Multi-View 3D Pedestrian Reconstruction Strategies for Urban Intersection Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00066)**  `arXiv:2611.00066`  
  _Kauan Mariani, Matheus Carvalho, Joel Perca, João Rulff, Jorge Poco_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Understanding how pedestrians move and interact at urban intersections is central to traffic-safety assessment, mobility planning, and smart-city sensing. Such analyses rely on physically grounded descriptions of motion: 3D body pose, metric trajectories, and pose-derived descriptors such as stature and walking speed. Recovering these from fixed roadside cameras is difficult: viewpoints are oblique and long-range, occlusions are frequent, and neither ground-truth 3D pose nor cross-camera identity labels are typically available. We compare two strategies for deriving pedestrian motion descriptors from a multi-camera intersection dataset: a monocular learned pipeline that combines text-prompted segmentation, tracking, and learned 3D body estimation, and a calibrated multi-view geometric pipeline that combines 2D pose estimation, tracking, cross-camera association, and triangulation. Because 3D ground truth is unavailable, we evaluate both with reference-free criteria relevant to intersection analysis: pedestrian coverage, anthropometric plausibility, walking-speed distributions, computational cost, and failure modes. The two strategies exhibit complementary trade-offs. The learned pipeline is simpler to deploy and covers more pedestrians, but suffers from scale ambiguity and systematic height compression; the geometric pipeline yields metric reconstructions more efficiently, but requires calibration, discards pedestrians seen by only one camera, and can produce severe outliers in dense crowds. We distill these findings into practical guidance for selecting a reconstruction strategy and configuring camera infrastructure according to the target analysis task.
  </details>

- **[BreastXAgent: A lightweight agentic explainability framework for breast density classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00065)**  `arXiv:2611.00065`  
  _Muhammad Turab, Raja Vavekanand, Knooz Fatima_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep learning models for breast density classification typically return only a label and confidence score. This paper presents BreastXAgent, a lightweight agentic framework that combines a pretrained classifier, Grad-CAM visual explanation, LangGraph-based routing, LLM report generation, and rule-based guardrails to produce controlled, faithful, non-diagnostic reports. On 160 mammography images, uncontrolled LLM reporting produced 75% Grad-CAM overclaims and 62.5% clinical overclaims. Strict prompting and LangGraph routing improved safety but did not eliminate violations. The full BreastXAgent achieved 100% safety pass rate, zero overclaims, and highest utility score. Results demonstrate that agentic guardrails enable safe, structured explanation generation without modifying the underlying classifier.
  </details>

- **[OpenMidnight: Closing the Performance Gap Between Open and Proprietary Pathology Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00064)**  `arXiv:2611.00064`  
  _Ratna Sagari Grandhi, Anis Chihoub, Ryan Kim, Daniel Z. Kaplan, Chao Feng, Anish Dulal, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pathology foundation models offer transferable representations for a range of downstream tasks in computational pathology, but reliance on proprietary data, substantial compute requirements, and limited availability of training code and preprocessing pipelines hinder independent validation and further methodological development. We present OpenMidnight 1.1, an open-source replication and refinement of Midnight trained on approximately 12,000 publicly available whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas. Using an encoder initialized with pretrained DINOv2 weights, OpenMidnight 1.1 uses approximately 320 H100 GPU-hours for pathology pretraining, a 34-fold reduction relative to the compute reported for Midnight. Across 16 classification and four segmentation datasets in THUNDER, OpenMidnight 1.1 achieves the highest mean segmentation Dice (69.7) and ranks fourth among 14 models, ahead of Midnight, with performance that matches or exceeds models trained on substantially larger datasets in several tasks. Our ablation studies additionally examine how initialization, data volume, model size, and tissue composition affect downstream performance, providing empirical evidence to inform the development of future training recipes. Our release of the training code, preprocessing pipeline, and model weights lowers barriers to reproducible research and further development of competitive pathology foundation models.
  </details>

- **[Where Generated Floor Plans Stop: Encoding Practice Acceptance Rules to Evaluate Machine Learning Floor Plan Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00063)**  `arXiv:2611.00063`  
  _Yiliang Shao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Machine learning floor plan generators are proposed as aids to design decisions, yet they are judged mainly by how closely a generated plan's room adjacencies match the request, a measure without architectural knowledge. We encode an architecture practice's floor plan acceptance rules, taken from its production layout software, as six checks applied in a fixed order, report each plan at the first check it fails, and calibrate the two room-shape limits, which no building code states, so that each alone rejects 5 per cent of built apartments. A transfer specification records which checks public data can carry. Applied to four published generators and two built corpora, RPLAN and Modified Swiss Dwellings (MSD), the checks stop the generators at different points. A room proportion check alone refuses 33.7 per cent of the House-GAN++ plans the checker can read and build, against 5.0 per cent of RPLAN, a gap that survives three measurement controls. At the 5 per cent rate, MSD apartments pass all six checks 5.5 to 23.5 points more often than House-GAN++, depending on the plans counted. The two generators that score best on the adjacency measure, Compatibility, pass least, because of how they represent plans, and within the two that pass most it barely predicts which plans pass. The checks thus expose what the standard measure misses; the checker is released. Passing is not shown to mean acceptance in practice.
  </details>

- **[CarDiff: Anatomically Aware Dental Caries Synthesis using Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00062)**  `arXiv:2611.00062`  
  _Sanyam Jain, Bruna Neves de Freitas, Alexandros Iosifidis, Ruben Pauwels_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Synthetic medical image generation can help address limited annotated data in dental imaging, particularly for under-represented caries classes. In this work, we present CarDiff, a semi-supervised framework for dental caries synthesis in panoramic radiographs. The method combines paired mask-image learning with self-supervised generation from augmented masks, while incorporating anatomy-aware conditioning between lesion regions and surrounding structures. Semantic consistency is enforced through segmentation-guided supervision and adversarial anatomical alignment. Experiments on the MLUA-DC1000 dataset show that CarDiff achieves improved synthesis quality compared with existing semantic synthesis baselines, obtaining the best Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) (90.76) and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) (0.48) scores among evaluated methods. We further assess the generated radiographs for downstream segmentation augmentation across seven architectures. Using a 5x augmented training set improves average Dice score by up to 6.5%, with larger gains observed for medium and combined lesion classes. These results suggest that anatomically consistent diffusion synthesis may be useful for dental radiograph augmentation under limited supervision. The code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[DDEL: Closed-Loop Mutual Enhancement of Dataset Distillation and Ensemble Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00061)**  `arXiv:2611.00061`  
  _Weiqi Zhang, Yongquan Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dataset distillation (DD) reduces a training set to a small set of examples, while ensemble learning (EL) combines predictions from several models. When applied in sequence, the distilled set remains fixed as the ensemble learns. We introduce DDEL, a framework that feeds ensemble behavior back into distillation. Each round trains the ensemble, measures loss and prediction disagreement on the source data, and uses these signals to guide the next data update. We implement this loop with distribution matching and a homogeneous three-member ensemble.Preliminary experiments cover skin lesion classification (ISIC 2019), treatment-response prediction (I-SPY1), and binary two-year prognosis classification (NSCLC-Radiomics). With the same images-per-class budget as the open-loop comparison, DDEL reaches balanced accuracy 0.3471 on ISIC and mean ROC-AUC 0.5120 and 0.5597 on I-SPY1 and NSCLC. The I-SPY1 difference is small, and the ISIC trajectory shows that more rounds do not consistently improve performance. These results offer initial evidence for studying DD-EL feedback, with its computational cost and robustness still requiring controlled evaluation.
  </details>

- **[CausalPrune: Counterfactual Causal Token Pruning for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00058)**  `arXiv:2611.00058`  
  _Pengcheng Zheng, Chaoning Zhang, Ya Wen, Jiaxin Huang, Jiaquan Zhang, Caiyan Qin, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in multimodal understanding, but their practical deployment is still limited by the substantial computation introduced by excessive visual tokens. Visual token pruning offers an effective solution by removing redundant visual tokens during inference. However, existing methods typically estimate token importance from correlational statistics, which cannot distinguish tokens that causally determine the model output from those spuriously associated with it. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{CausalPrune}, a counterfactual causal token pruning framework for efficient LVLMs. We formulate LVLM inference as a Structural Causal Model and introduce the Causal Token Importance Score (CTIS), which estimates the Average Treatment Effect of intervening on each visual token. To make causal estimation practical, we derive an efficient first-order approximation of CTIS and incorporate backdoor adjustment to mitigate latent cross-modal confounding. Within this causal formulation, layer-wise causal mediation decomposes token importance into direct and indirect effects through intermediate hidden states, enabling progressive pruning across transformer layers in a principled manner. Extensive experiments on various LVLM architectures, such as LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL, demonstrate that CausalPrune maintains comparable or even superior multimodal performance while achieving substantial reductions in FLOPs and prefill latency, consistently outperforming existing pruning methods.
  </details>

- **[SemaNorm: Stain Normalization via Semantic and Morphology Alignment for Robust Cross-Hospital Computational Pathology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00056)**  `arXiv:2611.00056`  
  _Subhankar Chattoraj, Sawon Pratiher, Arijit Ghosh, Prashant Khare, Writankar Kundu, Karan Vishwakarma, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Stain variability remains a major source of domain shift in computational pathology, yet existing normalization methods largely optimize color consistency without explicitly preserving morphology or diagnostic semantics. We propose SemaNorm, a self-supervised stain canonicalization stain normalizer to recover clean patches from strongly perturbed inputs, avoiding paired transfer, adversarial instability, and identity collapse. It further combines a frozen pathology foundation-model consistency loss with a differentiable nuclei-structure loss to preserve semantic and cellular organization. SemaNorm is evaluated across Camelyon17-WILDS and NCT-CRC-HE-100K using cross-hospital tumor classification, cell-graph morphology metrics, and semantic stability measured with an independent held-out foundation encoder. SemaNorm improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 5.9% over the strongest normalization baseline and by 13.5% over no normalization, while achieving the best morphology preservation. Independent foundation-model and cell-graph analyses further confirm improved semantic and structural stability. These results establish morphology- and semantics-aware optimization as a principled alternative to color-only stain normalization.
  </details>

- **[From Clips to Streams: A Unified Framework for Streaming Sign Language Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00055)**  `arXiv:2611.00055`  
  _Hoang Quan Dang, Xin Shen, Yanbin Liu, Xin Yu, Ling Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sign Language Translation (SLT) research has typically focused on pre-segmented clips, a constraint that disconnects models from the continuous reality of real-world communication. To bridge the gap from clips to streams, we formally define Streaming SLT, a realistic task demanding the joint discovery and translation of linguistic events from continuous, untrimmed video inputs. To address this challenge, we propose StreamSLST, the first end-to-end framework for Streaming Sign Language Segmentation and Translation via Deformable Transformer architecture. Unlike cascaded approaches that suffer from error propagation, StreamSLST employs a parallel decoding strategy to jointly optimize temporal segmentation and translation in a single pass. To enable scalable training on long-form videos, we incorporate a Sentence-aware Sliding Window Sampler that crops continuous streams into trainable units. We further design a Tri-modal Visual-Language Pretraining stage that aligns pose dynamics with textual semantics before joint optimization. To support comprehensive evaluation, we conduct experiments on two real-world streaming datasets, BOBSL and How2Sign, together with two newly constructed synthetic streaming benchmarks, Streaming-Phoenix-2014T and Streaming-CSL-Daily. The results demonstrate that StreamSLST consistently outperforms a matched cascaded segmentation-then-translation pipeline. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that joint optimization learns wider, translation-effective temporal support that simple expansion or rescaling of the annotated spans fails to reproduce. Our work establishes the first robust benchmark for continuous sign language understanding and paves the way for accessible real-world communication interfaces. The source code and data are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Auditing GeoFM Evaluation for Field-Extent Segmentation: Label Proxies, Baselines, and When Frozen Features Match Fine-tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00054)**  `arXiv:2611.00054`  
  _Santosh Pant_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Geospatial foundation-model (GeoFM) benchmarks for agricultural field-extent segmentation often rely on cropland land-cover proxies and compare against per-pixel spectral baselines. We measure how these choices affect conclusions using identical single-date Sentinel-2 pixels from six countries. Replacing polygon-derived field labels with ESA WorldCover cropland raises random-forest AUROC from 0.55-0.82 to 0.79-0.96, showing that the proxy creates a more spectrally separable task. On the actual field-extent labels, a from-scratch U-Net reaches 0.89-0.98 AUROC and has higher point AUROC than a Prithvi frozen linear probe in five of six regions. We then compare a frozen backbone and full fine-tuning using the same decoder for Prithvi and TerraMind, with ten matched seeds. At $\varepsilon=0.02$ AUROC, 9 of 12 region$\times$model cells are TOST-equivalent. Kenya is the common failure case: positives cover roughly 0.1% of pixels, and full fine-tuning performs better for both models. Cross-region results are less favorable to frozen models. On AUROC and average precision (AP), the U-Net leads the full 30-transfer matrix, while an exploratory analysis excluding Kenya finds that both frozen decoders outperform their fine-tuned counterparts; no AUROC difference is detected between frozen TerraMind and the U-Net in that subset. For Prithvi, a frozen decoder trains about $110\times$ fewer parameters than full fine-tuning. These results argue for auditing labels and baselines before interpreting GeoFM rankings, and for testing a frozen decoder before assuming that full fine-tuning will help. Our conclusions are limited to single-date, per-pixel field-extent segmentation, not parcel-boundary or instance delineation.
  </details>

- **[SIMIT: Self-Improving Vision-Language Models via Imagination at Test-Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00053)**  `arXiv:2611.00053`  
  _Mehmet Onurcan Kaya, Desmond Elliott, Dim P. Papadopoulos_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce SIMIT, a test-time self-improvement framework in which a vision-language model creates its own query-specific training data before answering an unlabeled test query. Our goal is to improve performance on a given target test set without annotations or external models. To pursue this goal, some test-time methods improve answers through longer reasoning or repeated sampling but leave the model unchanged. Others update the model using rewards based on majority agreement among multiple candidate answers or the model's own judgments of correctness, but such rewards can reinforce existing mistakes. SIMIT instead imagines similar problems whose solutions it controls: a model need not correctly solve the target query to construct useful practice examples. It synthesizes diverse (question, answer, image) triplets by specifying each answer before realizing its image. To support diverse multimodal tasks, SIMIT combines native image generation with an extensible skill library for structured visuals, including documents, charts, and diagrams. Within this pipeline, multi-stage verification checks that images support their assigned answers, while difficulty filtering retains informative examples. Adaptive budgeting further targets this practice by allocating more samples to queries the model is less confident in answering. The resulting data can improve the model in-context (SIMIT-ICL) or in-weight (SIMIT-FT). Across 17 diverse benchmarks, SIMIT outperforms existing self-improvement methods. Its best configuration achieves a +7.20% mean relative gain over BAGEL-7B, while training-free SIMIT-ICL achieves +6.98%.
  </details>

- **[ReactionBench: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Modeling Reactions to Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00050)**  `arXiv:2611.00050`  
  _Yibo Zhao, Ao Qu, Xuan Jiang, Jiahao Xu, Keane Ong, Hang Jiang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Understanding what happens in a video is not sufficient for socially responsive multimodal systems: such systems also aim to relate what a person observes to how that person responds. Existing video benchmarks largely evaluate events, temporal reasoning, or people depicted in the video, while affective and viewer-response datasets often focus on emotion labels, aggregate responses, or prediction from the stimulus alone. This leaves an underexplored question: can current multimodal models ground an observed viewer reaction in the stimulus context associated with it? We introduce ReactionBench, a human-anchored benchmark for reaction-specific video understanding. Built from a candidate pool of 31,834 synchronized stimulus-reaction clips spanning 433 hours and eight domains, ReactionBench evaluates three complementary abilities: ranking the intensity of a viewer's reactions within a video, matching a reaction to its temporally aligned stimulus, and explaining the concrete stimulus cues linked to that reaction. Human annotation provides 14,894 ratings over 3,257 moments, and the frozen evaluation comprises 250 intensity profiles, 112 matching items, and 200 rationale items with 447 blind-written human references. Across seven multimodal models, reaction-specific grounding remains challenging: the best model reaches 50.9% accuracy on four-way stimulus-reaction matching, while GPT-5 shows no detectable loss under reaction substitution. Performance is also sensitive to evaluation protocol. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Background Bias Assessment and Mitigation in Plant Disease Detection Using EfficientNet-B0 with Image Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00049)**  `arXiv:2611.00049`  
  _Majed Molhi, Nishi Gupta, Ali Algumaei_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Plant disease detection using deep learning has achieved remarkable accuracies exceeding 99% on benchmark datasets. However, these metrics may mask a critical vulnerability: models may be taking advantage of false background correlations instead of learning real pathological features. This study presents a systematic investigation of background bias in plant disease detection through a two-stage training framework with quantitative validation. We propose a three-condition evaluation protocol testing models on original, leaf-only, and background-only images to directly measure background dependency. Our approach combines standard transfer learning using EfficientNet-B0 and manipulation of background information during optimization. Experimental results on the PlantVillage dataset (20,638 images, 15 disease classes) show that while our model achieves 98.97% accuracy on the original images and maintains 96.62% accuracy on leaf-only images, the performance drops to 23.58% on background-only images. The calculated background bias (BBC) coefficient of 0.762 indicates that a large part of the model's predictive performance depends on leaf-related features rather than background distortions. This research offers clear evidence that even with the most advanced models, environmental shortcuts can be leveraged, and this highlights the importance of bias evaluation. The approach that has been used has laid a foundation for the development of agricultural AI that is ready for deployment. The implementation, models, and evaluation process are all publicly available.
  </details>

- **[Keyframes First, Motion Second: Revisiting Compressed-Domain Video Captioning under Limited Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00048)**  `arXiv:2611.00048`  
  _Asok B K, Ashim Nepal, Loknath Regmi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Compressed-domain video captioners such as CoCap read the H.264 bitstream directly: a pretrained encoder reads the keyframes (I-frames), while motion and residual encoders, trained from scratch, turn the codec's motion vectors and residuals into action tokens. This motion branch costs decoding time and supervision, both scarce on edge devices. We ask when it pays off under limited supervision. In a controlled study on 2,500 VATEX training clips, we fix a frozen SigLIP 2 keyframe encoder, a GPT-2 caption decoder and the training schedule, vary only the visual tokens the decoder receives (34 configurations), and report held-out test CIDEr with paired bootstrap intervals and three seeds. Motion encoders trained from scratch bring no measurable benefit: CoCap-style action tokens change CIDEr by -0.55 (95% CI [-2.3, +1.2]), and six other uses of motion do not help. Warm-started from a model trained on 48x the caption samples, they add +1.3 CIDEr on average, though not significantly across seeds, and only while the keyframe tokens stay frozen. Reading the keyframes better matters more: fine-tuning SigLIP 2's own attention-pooling head adds 5.4 CIDEr, and one to eight such tokens beat the 16 CoCap-style tokens on every seed while decoding only I-frames (7.3 ms instead of 44-114 ms per clip). The same holds on MSVD's full split in CoCap's own video encoding, where the readout leads by 14.2 CIDEr and action tokens bring no reliable gain, also with clean single-reference motion vectors. Under limited supervision, keyframes come first and motion second.
  </details>

- **[TopoMix: Continuous Spatial Mixing for Long-Tailed Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00047)**  `arXiv:2611.00047`  
  _Yefan Wang, Yusen Wu, Zihui Ling, Jianyuan Ni_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Most mixing-based augmentation methods improve generalization through a simple idea: combine two training samples with a fixed global ratio or a hard spatial replacement. While effective, this design leaves little room for local variation, which becomes a more visible limitation in long-tailed recognition, where minority classes are especially sensitive to the quality of augmented samples. We propose TopoMix, a training-free augmentation method that replaces fixed mixing with continuous spatial mixing. TopoMix constructs a smooth spatially varying mask from a low-resolution random control grid, bicubic interpolation, and stochastic non-linear shaping, and uses this mask for element-wise image mixing and label reweighting. Without introducing trainable parameters or auxiliary networks, TopoMix offers a simple way to make mixing more flexible in the input space. Experiments on standard long-tailed benchmarks show that it consistently improves over representative mixing-based baselines, indicating that smooth spatial mixing is an effective augmentation strategy for long-tailed recognition.
  </details>

- **[Circumpolar Wall-to-Wall Detection of Retrogressive Thaw Slumps with Scarce Labels and Extreme Class Imbalance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00046)**  `arXiv:2611.00046`  
  _Yili Yang, Heidi Rodenhizer, Robb Young, Brendan M. Rogers, Marlena Bartkus, Stefano Potter, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Retrogressive thaw slumps (RTS) are among the most dynamic ground deformations caused by permafrost thaw. Abrupt thaw processes such as RTS could roughly double the contribution of permafrost thaw to climate warming, and already threaten a third of Arctic infrastructure. Circumpolar RTS mapping has advanced quickly, yet released inventories together cover only part of the permafrost region. RTS occupy only 0.1-0.5% of image tiles and labels are costly, so a detector must be designed and evaluated as a rare-target problem. We therefore developed a deep learning system and mapped 20.68 M square kilometres of circumpolar permafrost using 41.6 M tiles of 4.8 m PlanetScope imagery. Training used 22,259 tiles with 2,609 RTS instances in 1,718 of them, and the model was tuned through 172 controlled experiments. A convolutional network matched every alternative tested, including multimodal fusion, foundation-model encoders and masked-autoencoder pretraining, each at far more compute for similar or worse results. Labelled data moved performance most, and a foundation model's advantage appeared only when labels were scarce. Tested once on held-out ecoregions at the real-world prevalence of 0.1-0.5%, the final model achieved an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.812-0.855, an object precision of 0.854 and F1 of 0.644. Deployed wall-to-wall, the model produced a circumpolar map of 19,068 high-confidence detections whose sampled precision ranges from 0.54 to 0.90 by size class. We present an evaluation protocol for rare targets, a controlled account of what governs accuracy under scarce labels, and the circumpolar RTS map the validated model produced.
  </details>

- **[Faces or Models? Where the Age Gap in Facial Expression Recognition Comes From](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00045)**  `arXiv:2611.00045`  
  _Jessica Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Facial expression recognition (FER) systems are increasingly used in elder care, yet their accuracy on older faces is rarely measured. This study evaluated five open-source FER models on the FACES database, which holds 2,052 posed photographs of 171 adults aged 19 to 80. The models cross three architectures (ResNet-18, POSTER++ and QCS) with two training datasets (RAF-DB and AffectNet). All models lost accuracy on older faces by 11.7 to 15.2 percentage points. Older faces were harder for people too: human raters lost 8.6 points, a classifier using only facial geometry lost 8.3, and for anger, fear, and happiness older adults differed more from one another when posing. On specific expressions the models fell much further than people did. AffectNet-trained models misread older neutral faces as sad or angry 62% of the time. RAF-DB-trained models lost fear, disgust, and anger instead. The gap persisted after controlling for architecture, image quality, cropping, and expression intensity. When only the final classification layer was refitted on older faces, the gap shrank from 11 to 21 points to 4 points or less, suggesting that the models' learned features can represent older faces and that the deficit lies in how the final layer was trained.
  </details>

- **[SparseWAM: Driving World-Action Models are Worth 16 Register Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00044)**  `arXiv:2611.00044`  
  _Yixiang Yang, Lizhong Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Zhiwen Chen, Jie Ling, Qiankun Yu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  World Action Models (WAMs) transfer scene-dynamics priors to planning by jointly forecasting future scenes and ego trajectories. However, WAMs built on video generators must generate dense future videos at inference, incurring prohibitive latency, while efficient variants discard the world branch at deployment and thus forgo test-time imagination. Even when dense video latents are replaced with patch-level DINO or JEPA features, these representations still involve long token sequences and encode decision-irrelevant information. We therefore propose SparseWAM, which forecasts in a sparse register space of only 16 tokens per frame, compressed from frozen DINOv2 features and shaped by joint planning-and-scoring pretraining to concentrate decision-relevant information. Within this space, SparseWAM employs a modality-decoupled Mixture-of-Transformers with a causal attention mask that lets action tokens condition on imagined future registers, retaining explicit imagine-then-act reasoning at deployment. Its compactness further enables low-cost multimodal sampling. As a result, our SparseWAM achieves 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 39.6 on NavHard at only 164 ms latency, roughly 1/5 that of DriveVA, demonstrating the efficiency of the sparse register space. Code will be released upon acceptance.
  </details>

- **[Diagnosing Zero-Shot Forgetting in CLIP Fine-Tuning: Attention Drift Characterizes Adaptation, Representation Drift Predicts Transfer Degradation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00042)**  `arXiv:2611.00042`  
  _Ruize Xia_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fine-tuning CLIP on a downstream task typically reduces its zero-shot accuracy on other tasks, and quantifying this loss ordinarily requires a labeled transfer benchmark. We study whether the loss can be anticipated from unlabeled target images that are already available during fine-tuning. Four signals are compared: the entropy of CLS token attention, linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) with the pretrained model, embedding drift, and relative weight change. ViT-B/32 is adapted by full fine-tuning (Full FT) and by LoRA on EuroSAT and Oxford-IIIT Pets over four learning rates and three seeds, with an additional ViT-B/16 grid; DTD and GTSRB are held out as confirmation targets, and forgetting is measured as zero-shot retention on CIFAR-100, Food-101, and ImageNet-R. Within a fixed configuration, the change in attention entropy is strongly associated with forgetting (mean $|\rho|=0.860$). Its sign, however, depends on the dataset, the adaptation method, and the backbone, and the pooled correlation falls to 0.361. A block decomposition shows that this sign is determined almost entirely by blocks 7 to 12. CKA ranks runs by retention at $\rho=0.960$, and the ranking is already established after the first of six epochs ($\rho=0.959$). On the held-out targets, CKA reaches $\rho=0.95$, and the block account correctly predicts the sign of the attention change for both datasets. These results support a simple decision rule: CKA is suited to comparisons across configurations, whereas attention entropy is informative only within a single configuration. The evidence is limited to one model family and short training schedules.
  </details>

- **[Think Before You Locate: Clinical Chain-of-Though Supervision for Sequential Medical Image Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00041)**  `arXiv:2611.00041`  
  _Adinath Madhavrao Dukre, Govinda Kolli, Yifan Lu, Ziyun Zou, Azmine Toushik Wasi, Sara Atito, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Clinicians rarely localize a finding from one image alone. They compare current and prior scans, follow structures across slices, and match regions across views or modalities. Yet vision-language models for sequential medical grounding usually learn only from bounding boxes. Boxes show where the target is, but they do not explain why that region in that image answers the question. We study whether explicit, image-grounded reasoning can improve localization, and which tasks benefit from it. We introduce method, whose core is MedChain, a corpus of 182,573 filtered rationales spanning eight sequential grounding tasks and ten imaging modalities. A medical VLM (FlemingVL-38B) first drafts a caption-like rationale, and a multimodal refiner (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) then re-examines the images, question and annotated box to write a box-conditioned explanation with explicit cross-image reasoning. We fine-tune Qwen3.5 on these rationales with deliberative chain-of-thought supervision (dCoT-SFT). Across 4B, 9B, and 27B models, dCoT-SFT sets a new state of the art on MedSG-Bench. The 27B model reaches 77.24 mIoU and 85.20 Acc@0.5, improving over the strongest prior model by 4.69 and 5.49 points. In a paired comparison using fixed 4B checkpoints, dCoT-SFT improves over answer-only SFT by 3.56 mIoU (95% CI 3.13--4.00). The gains mainly come from change detection and object tracking, while performance drops on three appearance-matching tasks. Replacing a model's own rationale with a rationale from another task reduces mIoU by 12.2 points, showing that localization depends strongly on the reasoning context. Finally, adding GRPO with an IoU reward after dCoT-SFT gives only small and task-dependent gains, which we analyze through controlled multi-seed development experiments.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Black Boxes: An Ontology Based Vision Framework for Transparent Fruit Disease Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00039)**  `arXiv:2611.00039`  
  _M.J. Marapperuma, B.V.K.I. Vidanage_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Efficiency and reliability in the timely identification of phytopathogens would help minimize crop loss in agricultural sectors but existing deep learning based methods, although accurate, would require a large annotated dataset and are black-boxed in their operation, thus, restricting flexibility and transparency. The current paper presents a hybrid detection framework that is able to overcome these drawbacks through the unified real-time vision with a semantic knowledge base. Web Ontology Language (OWL) was used to develop a comprehensive ontology of the disease of fruits that formally codifies phytopathological knowledge, such as symptom phenotype, spectral phenotype (HSV), and morphological phenotype. Such knowledge-guided configuration guides the image processing pipeline, making it possible to diagnose using this knowledge under expert specified rules without a large training dataset. The ontology underwent a computationally verified test of its structural soundness and commonsensical practical usefulness and scored an overall of 7.4/10. On the public set of MangoFruitDDS, the diagnostic performance was an F1 Score of 85.00%, precision of 85.00%, and a recall of 85.23%. These findings are very competitive and similar to other known deep learning models like the VGG16 that prove that the knowledge-driven approach provides an accurate, transparent, and scalable solution on automated fruit disease diagnosis.
  </details>

- **[Deep Learning for Detecting Building Setback Rule Violations in Urban Planning: A Case Study on Bangladesh](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00037)**  `arXiv:2611.00037`  
  _Farzana Tasnim, Faria Yasmin, Md. Tauseef-Ur-Rahman, Amina Islam, Tamzid Bin Tariq, Yuki Bhuiyan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dhaka's rapid urban growth has made building setback violations common, narrowing footpaths and blocking emergency access. RAJUK, responsible for building control in the Dhaka Metropolitan Area, enforces setback rules mainly through manual field inspection, which scales poorly. We present a systematic comparison of four machine learning approaches for classifying building setback conditions from street-level photographs: negative (compliant), moderate (borderline), and positive (violation). We built a labeled dataset of 372 geo-tagged images from sixteen Dhaka neighborhoods and expanded it with 5,968 augmented copies for training. We trained and evaluated a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), a Random Forest ensemble on frozen ResNet50 embeddings, a support vector machine on frozen ResNet18 embeddings, and a fine-tuned ResNet18 CNN. On a 1,275-image test set, the fine-tuned CNN achieved 65.4% accuracy (macro-F1 0.50), followed by Random Forest at 59.9% (macro-F1 0.44) and SVM at 58.2% (macro-F1 0.45). All models classify the compliant class reliably but struggle with the borderline moderate class due to visual ambiguity. These results establish reference performance levels for automated setback-compliance screening in a South Asian regulatory setting.
  </details>

- **[From Single-Shot QA to Continuous Perception: Revisiting the Energy Composition and Optimization Boundary of Edge VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00036)**  `arXiv:2611.00036`  
  _Yiting Duan, Miaoxin Wang, Aoqing Guo, Bo Peng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visual-prefill energy conclusions for edge vision-language models (VLMs) are commonly drawn under single-shot workloads; we revisit them under continuous perception. Profiling nine VLMs across three architecture families on Jetson AGX Thor and Orin (4,508 records, calibrated with a pure-text task), we find two mutually independent energy laws: the per-output-token decode cost grows monotonically with model scale, whereas the visual-prefill (image-encoding) cost is dominated by visual-encoder architectural efficiency, not scale. Under continuous perception ($N{=}10$) with sparse output, visual-prefill energy reaches 92--97\% of total. We derive optimization strategies---visual frame reuse, adaptive output truncation, task-aware routing, and encoder throughput optimization---for edge VLM deployment.
  </details>

- **[Selective Positional Allocation for Noise-Robust Query Retrieval in Small-Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00035)**  `arXiv:2611.00035`  
  _Yangchen Zeng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In aerial and remote-sensing imagery, detecting tiny targets is frequently hampered less by the representational capacity of the backbone network than by the manner in which positional priors are distributed across ill-defined foreground and background regions. We introduce SPAR (Selective Positional Allocation and Retrieval), a detection framework that re-conceptualizes positional cues as an allocatable resource: they are intensified at semantically meaningful locations while responses driven by scene clutter are actively attenuated. At the heart of SPAR lies Selective Positional Embedding (SPE), an interpretable embedding mechanism paired with an activation-bar visualization that facilitates direct inspection and hyper-parameter tuning.
