On GB300 hardware, experiments with Qwen3 (235B) show approximately 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4 while maintaining near-Native-FP4 serving throughput. Under memory-constrained prefix reuse, P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5%. These results demonstrate software-based reconstruction on existing FP4 hardware and inform the development of future MX-native inference systems.
  </details>

- **[On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00350)**  `arXiv:2611.00350`  
  _Anirudh Buvanesh, Khaled Rouissi, Sujin Yun, Johan Obando-Ceron, Morgane M Moss, Samuel Lavoie, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.
  </details>

- **[DEPLOY-RL: Active Boundary Discovery and Conservative Certification for Deployable Reinforcement Learning in Safety-Critical Continuous Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00342)**  `arXiv:2611.00342`  
  _Yeojin Jang, Minu Baek, Gihun Gil, Minsung Jung, Beomdo Park, Woohyeon Kwon, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning (RL) policies often outperform classical controllers in simulation, yet rarely reach production in safety-critical processes. The barrier is that there is no principled way to answer "Is this policy safe to deploy?" with statistical guarantees. We introduce DEPLOY-RL, a post-training certification framework built on one key insight: deployment certification requires discovering where failures occur (boundary discovery), not measuring how much everywhere (uniform reconstruction). Our contributions: (1) a contract-coupled acquisition function that concentrates sampling on certification-critical boundaries, achieving approximately 2x sample efficiency with a semi-empirical ambiguity reduction bound (domain-calibrated convergence guarantee); (2) conformal risk control providing finite-sample false-go guarantees (<= alpha) under explicit deployment contracts; (3) a three-way decision framework (Deploy/No-Deploy/Abstain) with fail-safe PID/MPC fallback. In simulations on papermaking (industrial digital twin) and Tennessee Eastman (public benchmark), DEPLOY-RL achieves 4.4% false-go rate (vs. 8.6% for the best baseline) while retaining 88.6% policy coverage, the only method achieving <5% false-go with >85% coverage among 14 baselines under our evaluation protocol.
  </details>

- **[Decomposing Irregular Time Series into Interpretable Temporal Patterns with Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00337)**  `arXiv:2611.00337`  
  _Jenna L. Ballard, Zijie Pan, Shivani Shekhar, Yiming Bian, Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Avinash Thangali, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Irregularly-spaced sequential data, such as transaction logs, encode multi-scale temporal structure that is critical for prediction but difficult to recover explicitly with standard sequence models, which often trade interpretability for performance. We introduce MoTIF, an interpretable framework using mixture-of-experts (MoE) attention to decompose irregular time series into temporal patterns spanning minute-to-year scales. Each expert is trained via temporal alignment that induces attention specialization to a designated cyclical or within-range pattern, with label-free routing supervision that learns to activate the correct expert from patterns present in the data. On synthetic data with known temporal structure, MoTIF recovers correct routing well above chance (0.389/0.829 for range/cyclical patterns vs. 0.091 random) and outperforms all baselines, including a standard transformer and an unspecialized MoE, on next-value prediction. On a public credit card transaction dataset, MoTIF achieves higher macro-F1 than all baselines for next-amount prediction. Its learned routing reveals structure a black-box model cannot: transactions are governed primarily by intraday and short-interval rhythms, while fraudulent transactions show bursty, calendar-agnostic timing versus the steadier periodicity of legitimate ones. On downstream fraud detection, MoTIF matches standard transformer and MoE baselines and clearly outperforms recent sequential recommendation models used as embedding baselines. These results show that decomposing temporal structure into interpretable, expert-specific patterns need not sacrifice predictive accuracy, offering a practical route to sequence models that are both accurate and auditable in high-stakes settings. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Cyber-physical attack detection approaches in the wide-area measurement system](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00316)**  `arXiv:2611.00316`  
  _Zakaria El Mrabet, Prakash Ranganathan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Improving situational awareness within the Smart Grid is an effective preventive measure to detect potential anomalies, and avoid their adverse consequences. A wide area measurement system (WAMS) based Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) can assist in improving visibility within the grid by collecting relevant measurements including magnitude, phase angle, frequency, voltage, and current, with a precise GPS-based timestamp. So far, there are more than 2500 PMUs deployed in the North American power grid, where each of which generates between 30 and 60 samples/s, roughly 1.5 TB/month of streamed data. Thus, processing such large PMU streams requires expensive computational resources and faster algorithms. This paper provides state-of-the-art cyber and physical anomalies in the WAMS and analyses their impact on the integrity and availability of the system. Next, it investigates the current anomaly detection approach in historical and streaming PMU data, including conventional machine learning and hybrid approaches, and assesses their advantages and main drawbacks. Lastly, it sheds light on the importance of handling missing PMU data and concept drifts.
  </details>

- **[RaMMOBO: Random Max-Margin Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00312)**  `arXiv:2611.00312`  
  _Thomas Wedenig, Paul Plantosar, Robert Peharz_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) maximizes $M$ expensive black-box objectives with the goal of approximating the Pareto set, whose objective vectors cannot be improved in one component without sacrificing another. A common quality measure is hypervolume, the volume in objective space dominated by these vectors relative to a reference point. Expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) directly targets this metric and is one-step Bayes-optimal, but its standard computation scales exponentially with $M$, making it prohibitively expensive for many-objective problems. We introduce random max-margin multi-objective Bayesian optimization (RaMMOBO), whose acquisition function lower-bounds EHVI while requiring only linear cost in $M$ to evaluate. RaMMOBO measures the volume of a max-margin box contained in a candidate's hypervolume-improvement region and averages over random reweightings of the objective space, yielding a utility that is strictly Pareto-monotone on hypervolume-improving outcomes. It naturally handles noisy observations and different probabilistic surrogates and supports efficient gradient-based optimization. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, RaMMOBO matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with largest gains at higher $M$, with acquisition optimization up to two orders of magnitude faster than qLogNEHVI. Our implementation is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Quantization of Large Models with Weight Outliers and Sparsity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00286)**  `arXiv:2611.00286`  
  _Leonidas Tsigkounakis, Abraham Jaeger Mountain, Yilang Zhang, Georgios B. Giannakis_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.
  </details>

- **[OCELOT: Planetary-Scale Species Distribution Modeling with Satellite Foundation Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00284)**  `arXiv:2611.00284`  
  _Bart van Merriënboer, Lauren Harrell, Keith Anderson, Burcu Karagol Ayan, Elise Kleeman, Tom Denton, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large-scale repositories of species observations now contain billions of occurrence records from around the world, but these sightings cluster heavily in human-accessible areas. Existing models use only a small fraction of these records and are not evaluated on extrapolating to remote, unvisited regions--where species distribution models can be used as geographic priors to help classify data from camera traps and acoustic recorders. We scale relative occurrence species distribution models by training a multimodal implicit neural representation network called OCELOT that fuses spatial coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings on two orders of magnitude more observations than previous work: 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Scaling to this regime requires co-designing the data pipeline, taxonomic representation, loss formulation, and model architecture: spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling correct for spatial redundancy and observer bias, while an additive taxonomic readout shares representations across species, genera, and families to improve predictions for rare taxa. To evaluate performance in remote areas, we benchmark geographic extrapolation using the NDCG metric on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km. Satellite foundation embeddings improve extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The resulting model also matches or outperforms existing baselines on established interpolation benchmarks, demonstrating that optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy.
  </details>

- **[DELBERT-2: Pretrained Fingerprint Language Models for DEL Protein Binder Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00281)**  `arXiv:2611.00281`  
  _Bing Hu, Sun Sun, Shaik Salman Basha, Anita Layton, Helen Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present DELBERT-2, a pretrained fingerprint language model that converts sparse molecular fingerprints into unified token sequences using a ModernBERT encoder trained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus. We evaluate across six targets (WDR91, WDR12, SETDB1, PLCZ1, LRRK2, DCAF7) under three out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols: hierarchical cluster splits probe chemical novelty, library splits test cross-library transfer, and building-block splits assess compositional generalization. DELBERT-2 consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 relative to LightGBM ensemble baselines and transformers trained from scratch, with the largest gains in stringent OOD regimes. DELBERT-2 achieves 13.28+/-3.72 enrichment factor at top-100 vs. 12.36+/-3.75 for no-pretraining (p=0.040), representing 7.4% improvement and 13x enrichment over random selection. These results demonstrate that fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning effectively improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, enabling practical DEL virtual screening. Code is available at \hyperlink{this https URL}{DELBERT-2}.
  </details>

- **[IsoAlign: Isoform-Aware DNA-Protein Alignment via Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00241)**  `arXiv:2611.00241`  
  _Niousha Sadjadi, Arman Seyed-Ahmadi, Tony Tu, Micaela Elisa Consens, Kerr Ding, Alif Munim, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Genomic foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning DNA sequence representations, yet existing self-supervised pretraining strategies overlook alternative splicing and underperform compared to specialized models. To address this gap, we introduce IsoAlign, a multimodal framework that grounds genomic pretraining in isoform-aware DNA-protein alignment to learn biologically meaningful representations. IsoAlign aligns transcripts to their corresponding protein isoforms, capturing both coding sequences and broader regulatory contexts, using two Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA): DNA-Protein JEPA (DP-JEPA), which predicts protein representations from DNA using contrastive alignment, and Isoform-Masked JEPA (IM-JEPA), which models relationships among alternative isoforms of the same gene through masked protein prediction. We evaluate the learned DNA representations of these architectures across a multi-metric evaluation suite spanning tasks, including the prediction of pathogenicity, fitness, gene expression, and TF binding. Our results demonstrate that isoform-aware cross-modal alignment using JEPA significantly improves functional representations and downstream performance, establishing a promising direction for GFM pretraining.
  </details>

- **[Interpretable structural temperature scaling for calibrating graph neural networks and point-cloud segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00175)**  `arXiv:2611.00175`  
  _Chenyi Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Graph-aware calibrators make graph neural networks (GNNs) more trustworthy by predicting a temperature for each node, usually with auxiliary networks whose decisions are hard to inspect. We propose Interpretable Structural Temperature Scaling (ISTS), a twelve-parameter linear model that sets each node's temperature from named descriptors of its confidence, neighbourhood and closeness to labelled nodes, so every temperature traces back to descriptor contributions. ISTS preserves predictions, and cross-validated regularisation lets the calibration data decide how far the model departs from temperature scaling (TS). Its explanations are faithful at the level of node groups: on test nodes, ISTS softens groups that a global temperature leaves over-confident and sharpens under-confident ones (Spearman correlation 0.67 over 246 groups). On seven graphs with two backbones and eleven baselines, ISTS has the best average rank in negative log-likelihood (NLL) and Brier score and lowers NLL relative to TS by 1.8%, more than twice the gain of an identically fitted entropy-based temperature. It ranked first again on four held-out graphs under a protocol fixed in advance. From about 100 calibration nodes on, ISTS is a cheap and inspectable choice, and on point-cloud segmentation it significantly improves NLL, Brier score and the ranking of points for rejection.
  </details>

- **[FB-MOAC: A Reinforcement Learning Algorithm for Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00130)**  `arXiv:2611.00130`  
  _Mohsen Amidzadeh, Mario Di Francesco_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are effective in solving problems that can be modeled as Markov decision processes (MDPs).These algorithms primarily target forward MDPs whose dynamics evolve over time from an initial state.However, several important problems in different scenarios including stochastic control and network systems exhibit both a forward and a backward dynamics. As a consequence, they cannot be expressed as a standard MDP, thereby callingfor a novel theory for RL in this context.Accordingly, this work introduces the concept of Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes (FB-MDPs)for multi-objective problems,develops a novel theoretical framework to characterize their optimal solutions,and proposes a general forward-backward step-wise templatethat allows to adapt RL algorithms for FB-MDP problems.A Forward Backward Multi Objective Actor Critic (FB-MOAC) algorithm is introduced accordinglyto obtain optimal policies with guaranteed convergence and a competitive rate with respect to standard approaches in RL.FB-MOAC is evaluated on diverse use cases in the context of mathematical finance and mobile resource management.The obtained results show that FB-MOAC outperforms the state of the art across different metrics,highlighting its ability to learn and maximize rewards.
  </details>

- **[Output-Aware Block Influence: Jacobian-Lens Weighting for Depth Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00015)**  `arXiv:2611.00015`  
  _Kyle Lemoi, Jonathan Yong, Shubhankar Tripathy, Priestley Fernandes, Anirban Majumder, Zarreen Reza_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Depth pruning removes entire transformer blocks and therefore depends on a reliable criterion for identifying which blocks can be removed. Block Influence (BI) ranks blocks by how minimally they rotate the hidden state. However, local redundancy does not necessarily imply downstream irrelevance. We address this limitation using the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens) neural artifact, a map transporting perturbations at a layer to the final residual stream. At a common sparsity level, pruning scores applying J-Lens transportation to $BI$, what we call $J-BI$, were found to improve post-pruning accuracy by up to 19 points over $BI$ while reducing damage to perplexity for Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-IT, and Gemma-3-12B-IT. We also perform a single-block ablation study and use J-Lens probing to explain why the proposed scores improved performance.
  </details>

- **[Generated storm lifecycles fill the rare-event tail of short rainfall records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.41365)**  `arXiv:2610.41365`  
  _Valerie Tsao, Nathaniel W. Chaney, Manolis Veveakis, Marta Zaniolo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Historically rare ''one-in-a-generation'' storms are occurring with unprecedented frequency, causing catastrophic damage and mounting casualties, and exposing the vulnerability of infrastructure designed around short observational records. To overcome the limitations of sparse data, we present StormGen, a generative machine-learning model that transforms an observed storm's initial hours into complete, physically plausible hourly rainfall lifecycles in minutes. Evaluated on a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, StormGen produced close counterparts for 4\5% of the most severe 2\% of storms--compared to just 3\% for stochastic storm transposition--and maintained spatial coherence over full 24-hour sequences. Crucially, from a single hour of initial rainfall, the model successfully reconstructed the specific lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey itself, despite the event being entirely absent in training. Because storm timing alone can more than double peak flows, these complete generated scenarios provide a vital mechanism to stress-test flood protections against unprecedented extremes.
  </details>

- **[SPT-Flow: One Integration, Many Futures in Continuous-Time World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.41273)**  `arXiv:2610.41273`  
  _Mingyang Lyu, Yinqian Sun, Gongce Cao, Yuhao Zhang, Lu Jia, Qian Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Continuous-time world models generate a latent trajectory through a single ODE integration, but adding stochastic conditioning does not ensure that the model uses it. In our teacher-forced baseline, posterior means vary by only about 1% of the prior scale, and matched and swapped latents yield indistinguishable reconstruction PSNR at the reported precision. We study a supervision-shortcut hypothesis: ground-truth intermediate states can reduce the need for trajectory-associated latent information. We introduce SPT-Flow, which samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at multiple readout times. Re-anchoring experiments support the proposed mechanism. On LIBERO, with both models trained for 30k optimizer steps, SPT-Flow improves best-of-10 PSNR over our retrained ODEWorld baseline by 2.0 and 2.4 dB at the mid-trajectory and final frames and reduces mean LPIPS by 23%, with comparable per-sample inference cost. The rollout control recovers most of the accuracy gain; learned latent conditioning adds diversity and best-of-K gains while reducing mean sample accuracy relative to this control. The diagnostics support trajectory-associated latent utilization; semantic mode coverage under matched conditions in the robotic setting remains unverified.
  </details>

- **[D-MOD: Diffusion mode estimation for accelerated MRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40110)**  `arXiv:2610.40110`  
  _Md Kawsar Ahmed, Mathews Jacob_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion models are powerful priors for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but most current methods are posterior samplers, which return a random draw from the posterior. A reproducible and high-quality reconstruction often requires averaging many samples, resulting in a high computational cost. We introduce D-MOD, a fast algorithm that instead provides a posterior mode. It uses a minorize-maximize algorithm on a lower bound of the smoothed log-posterior, which provably increases the objective. Each iteration draws S noisy samples of the current estimate at the current noise level, denoises them with a pretrained diffusion model, and combines their average with the measured k-space through a conjugate-gradient (CG) solve. We anneal the noise levels, as the distance between the bound and its target decays quadratically with noise. On fastMRI brain (T1, T2, FLAIR), a single D-MOD reconstruction exceeds, in PSNR, the 10-sample finite-MMSE estimates of DPS, DAPS and SNORE-P and stays within 0.31 dB of the strongest baselines (DiffPIR, DDS). This approach thus provides a fast deterministic reconstruction algorithm (11-73 times faster than MMSE estimates), which is useful in a clinical setting.
  </details>

- **[Possibility-based Inference: A Deterministic Framework for Robust and Reliable Uncertainty Quantification in Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39821)**  `arXiv:2610.39821`  
  _Seyedfakhredin Musavishavazi, Maryam Alipour_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Decision-making under uncertainty remains a key issue in Machine Learning (ML), particularly in the deployment of safety-critical systems, where reliable quantification of system behavior is essential for evaluating behavioral impacts and strengthening confidence in ML models. This contribution, influenced by fuzzy set theory and grounded in Bayesian statistics, addresses challenges related to data precision and the performance-accuracy trade-off in Bayesian inference (BI). To this end, we introduce a possibility-based contrastive grade of prediction as an alternative quantification method to existing latent posterior-based approaches for parameter estimation (approximation) and model selection. Unlike conventional Bayesian inference, which represents uncertainty within the probabilistic framework, the proposed model adopts a possibility-based representation that allows uncertain and potentially conflicting information to be characterized more flexibly. Rather than focusing on isolated aspects of a problem, the resulting mathematical framework provides a systematic approach to data mining while mitigating overly confident, yet implausible predictions generated by highly specialized deep learning architectures.
  </details>

- **[Causal Attention on CPU: A Cache-Aware and Load-Balanced Scheduling Kernel for Prefill](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38809)**  `arXiv:2610.38809`  
  _Kwun Fung Lau, Frost Mitchell, Kanya Mo, Emani Ashok_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agentic AI drives significant productivity gains across diverse domains, but concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute resources. Although CPUs offer a viable alternative, existing CPU attention kernels fall short in adapting to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling. To address this, we introduce CACPU, a high-performance attention kernel featuring tiered cache blocking and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism designed for causal full-sequence prefilling. CACPU achieves up to a 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.
  </details>

- **[The Role of Quantization in Loss Spikes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38277)**  `arXiv:2610.38277`  
  _Zaiqian Chen, Aditya Somasundaram, Sophie Li, Sean McLeish, John Kirchenbauer, Tom Goldstein, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Loss spikes in language model pretraining can waste substantial compute and derail otherwise healthy training runs. A primary driver of these instabilities is the growth and divergence of output logits in the final language modeling (LM) head. In this work, we study a particularly costly form of this instability associated with output logit growth: delayed, terminal divergences that emerge only after prolonged training, which we call time-bomb spikes. We find that these instabilities are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head, which eventually culminates in a loss spike. Crucially, reducing numerical precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while increasing precision improves stability. We then propose a simple yet effective mitigation that replaces AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum, suppressing logit growth and improving stability over long training horizons. Finally, we find that existing mitigation techniques from the literature (along with our own) all reduce quantization error, suggesting a shared numerical mechanism behind their effectiveness. Together, our results identify finite precision error as a hidden driver of time-bomb spikes and show that suppressing this error is key to stable long-horizon pretraining.
  </details>

- **[NAGO: Noise-Aware Generative Operator via Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38273)**  `arXiv:2610.38273`  
  _Guanyu Chen, Shengze Xu, Pengwei Liu, Xingyu Ren, Pengkai Wang, Antonios Armaou, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce NAGO, a noise-aware generative operator for efficient sampling from invariant measures of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) in function space. Our central idea is to treat the source measure as a design variable rather than a fixed Gaussian default. We establish admissibility conditions for well-defined infinite-dimensional flows and show that the finite-band source--target covariance ratio controls the spectral stiffness of the marginal velocity field. This analysis yields an admissibility-constrained spectral-matching rule: choose a source that is sufficiently rough for well-posedness, then minimize covariance mismatch over the resolved Fourier modes. On three representative stochastic-field benchmarks, this source design improves few-step spectral accuracy and several complementary distributional and physical statistics. In a controlled Matern-field ablation, it reduces the accurate RK4 budget from about 30 steps for Gaussian functional flow matching to 3--5 steps, a $6$--$10\times$ reduction in neural ODE evaluations. These gains are strongest for stationary multiscale fields and depend on the metric, resolution, and guidance protocol.
  </details>

- **[B2P-Corr: Batch-to-Population Gradient Estimators for Non-Decomposable Correlation Losses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38171)**  `arXiv:2610.38171`  
  _Jingquan Yan, Yuwei Miao, Peiran Yu, Junzhou Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Correlation metrics such as the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) and Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) are standard regression metrics and learning objectives, but their non-decomposable nature poses a challenge for stochastic optimization. Since these metrics depend on dataset-level moments (mean, variance, covariance), naive mini-batch training with local statistics yields biased, high-variance gradients whose expectation does not align with the population gradient. To bridge this ``batch-to-population'' (B2P) gap, we propose B2P-Corr, a novel framework that transforms correlation objectives into decomposable pseudo-losses driven by lightweight global ``moment sketches''. We introduce two efficient variants: B2P-EMA, which utilizes exponential moving averages and stop-gradient operators to ensure asymptotic gradient tracking with $O(B)$ cost ($B$ is batch size); and B2P-U, which uses sampled cross-batch U-statistic estimators and a reservoir-based stabilization with an $O(B)$ implementation. Theoretically, we quantify the $O(B^{-1})$ bias of naive mini-batch optimization, prove a moving-target tracking result for B2P-EMA under a fast-sketch / slow-parameter regime, and provide an idealized control-variate analysis for B2P-U. Experiments on two synthetic and three real-world datasets demonstrate B2P-Corr achieves stable optimization and higher correlation than naive mini-batch optimization with negligible overhead.
  </details>

- **[Simulated petrological labels enable probabilistic mineralogy prediction from whole-rock geochemistry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36429)**  `arXiv:2610.36429`  
  _Matthew J. Liu, Aaron D. Kaplan, Michael L. Whittaker, Kristin A. Persson_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modal mineralogy, the mineral identities and abundances in rocks, guides geological studies and industrial resource extraction. While measuring modal mineralogy is time-intensive, whole-rock chemical measurements furnish elemental concentrations at higher throughput. Predicting mineralogy from elemental data, however, poses a one-to-many inverse problem, and labeled mineralogical datasets are too sparse to train on at scale. We address both challenges by simulating petrological labels that express multiple formation conditions per composition and at a scale unattainable by measurements. Nearly one million simulated labels supervise the middle component of a three-part model: a transformer encoder self-supervised on roughly 788,000 whole-rock compositions, the simulation-trained heads that predict distributions over mineral assemblages, and a recalibration layer that aligns the predictions with measured mineralogy. Zero-shot on 640 volcanic rocks, the model discriminates the presence of most mineral categories and predicts which rocks are richer in each mineral. However, the predicted abundances are systematically offset from measured values. Recalibration fit on as few as 25 labeled rocks recovers 76 percent of the likelihood improvement from fitting on the full 368-rock fitting set, while abundance error responds more slowly (11.0% zero-shot and 9.5% with the full fitting set). This work demonstrates how a machine learning model in the geochemical sciences can both leverage an imperfect simulator and mitigate its systematic biases.
  </details>

- **[Gaussian Approximation for Composition and Subsampling of Differentially Private Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33333)**  `arXiv:2610.33333`  
  _Vitaly Feldman, Moshe Shenfeld_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The privacy analysis of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) relies on bounds for the composition of subsampled mechanisms. The privacy of such a composition is bounded by that of a pair of product distributions, whose privacy loss is a sum of independent terms and has been analyzed via a variety of notions and concentration results. Yet, existing closed-form bounds either lose a logarithmic factor or require restrictive conditions on the noise scale and delicate analysis of subsampling. Further, while it is well known that sums of independent random variables are approximately Gaussian, existing CLT-based techniques give an approximation with a large error in $\delta$.We show that the privacy loss of this pair is approximately Gaussian as long as each step has a small privacy loss except with small probability. Specifically, its privacy loss distribution is close to a Gaussian with the same mean and variance, after truncating the rare large privacy losses. The closeness in both directions is up to a shift of $\varepsilon$ that grows only as $\ln(1/\beta)$ for an additive error $\beta$ in $\delta$ and is a lower-order term in typical applications. In particular, the composition satisfies Gaussian differential privacy up to a lower-order shift of $\varepsilon$ and the additive error $\beta$. We also give a simple way to analyze the resulting variance-based bounds for subsampled mechanisms which relies on the $\chi^2$ divergence of a single step. For the Gaussian mechanism at sampling rate $1/t$ and $t>\ln^{3}(1/\delta)$, this gives the predicted rate for $\sigma\gtrsim\max\{1,\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/\ln(t)\}$, whereas the standard Rényi-divergence analyses need $\sigma\gtrsim\sqrt{t\ln(1/\delta)}/\ln(t)$. We extend these results to random allocation (balls-and-bins sampling), and show that it explains the high accuracy of the connect-the-dots method.
  </details>

- **[Tree Depth and Sample-Quality-Associated Features: Two Hidden Factors in Boruta Selection for RNA-Seq Data Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33307)**  `arXiv:2610.33307`  
  _Tareque Mohmud Chowdhury, Abu Raihan Mostofa Kamal_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Random Forest--based selectors such as Boruta depend on tree depth, yet Boruta's most used implementation, BorutaPy, recommends depths of 3 to 7 without published evidence. We tested the effect of depth using pan-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (10,469 tumors, 33 cancer types) and breast cancer PAM50 subtyping (981 tumors, 5 subtypes). Label-dependent steps were fitted inside training folds, effects were measured against seed-to-seed variation, and each task kept a locked test set. In pan-cancer data, depth 5 changed the selection far more than a new seed did: the top-500 Jaccard overlap with unlimited depth was 0.37, against 0.84 (depth 5) and 0.93 (unlimited) between seeds. Depth-5 trees confirmed 472 instead of 1,659 genes, covered fewer large-class markers (16% vs 62%) and gave less accurate 50-gene panels (balanced accuracy 0.809 vs 0.889). The effect vanished once the cap reached 61 to 76% of the median depth of unrestricted trees, a depth that depends mainly on the number of classes, not sample size. In PAM50 subtyping (median depth 12) the effect was small, and leaving depth uncapped cost no accuracy in either task. It replicated in a second cross-validation repeat and under permutation importance. About a third of pre-filtered candidates correlated within class with the number of detected genes, a sample-quality measure; a within-class filter removed them without loss of test accuracy (0.943 vs 0.942 balanced accuracy, 1,000 genes). We recommend uncapped trees, or a cap above 75% of the realized median depth, and a within-class quality filter before Boruta.
  </details>

- **[RadonBench: A Benchmark of Classical and Learning-Guided Search Techniques for Problems in Combinatorial Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33259)**  `arXiv:2610.33259`  
  _Xiaoan Xu, Jesus A. De Loera, Ethan X. Fang, Junwei Lu, Luze Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Classical optimization and learning-guided search offer complementary approaches to open problems in discrete mathematics, but their outputs are difficult to compare when search spaces, validity checks, and stopping rules differ. We present \emph{RadonBench}, a benchmark for constructing maximum-cardinality Radon-free lattice configurations: finite subsets of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ admitting no integral Radon partition. It remains open whether Radon-free configurations with $11$ points in $\mathbb{Z}^3$ or $21$ points in $\mathbb{Z}^4$ are possible. If they exist, they would improve the corresponding lower bounds on the integer Radon numbers. We compare exhaustive extension, greedy local search, PatternBoost, AlphaZero, and AlphaEvolve. All outputs use one success predicate: a convex target-sized configuration succeeds exactly when its number of integral Radon points is zero. PatternBoost and AlphaZero construct verified Radon-free configurations of sizes $10$ and $20$, one point short of the respective targets; AlphaZero's best convex target terminals have two integral Radon points in both dimensions. Exhaustive extension over fixed seeds and declared finite search boxes likewise reaches a minimum of two integral Radon points. Greedy local search and AlphaEvolve each produce target-sized near misses with one integral Radon point. No audited run reaches zero. These results establish reproducible near-miss baselines over explicitly scoped search domains.
  </details>

- **[CIS-Transolver: A Cross-layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26337)**  `arXiv:2610.26337`  
  _Jianglong Liu, Zhicheng Zhu, Jia Hao, Liangyue Jia, Wenxuan He_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to predicting complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias limits their ability to reconstruct fine-scale flow variations around geometric features such as side mirrors and wheel arches. Reliable assessment of local geometric changes therefore requires models that capture fine spatial detail together with global flow interactions. Inspired by iterative refinement and state evolution, we propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that integrates local multiscale information into global flow modeling. The method extracts local feature variations and encodes them as zeroth- to second-order geometric moments. These encodings are combined with information from earlier layers to form a cross-layer memory. Memory-derived corrections enter the value branch of Physics-Attention, allowing local details to inform global physical-state interactions throughout the network. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. Relative error reductions average 8.72% compared with the best baseline for each metric. Also achieves the lowest high-frequency spectral errors across all five metrics, with an average relative reduction of 16.06% compared with the best baseline. These results support cross-layer reuse of local information for fine-scale automotive flow prediction.
  </details>

- **[Certifiable inversion of resampling-induced spectral distortion in high-dimensional particle filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23448)**  `arXiv:2610.23448`  
  _Deming Song, Chi-Kin Lam, Kefeng Li, Hui Yu, Xilin Li, Huagang Lin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper formulates and solves the inverse problem of recovering the pre-resampling spectrum of a particle filter's ensemble covariance from the importance weights and the observed spectrum alone. Resampling controls weight degeneracy, but in high dimensions it also distorts that spectrum: the distortion is a free multiplicative convolution with a law computable from the weights, so the repair is a deconvolution. We first extend the forward spectral law to random importance weights by conditioning on the weights together with the realized offspring counts rather than on the weights alone, which makes the distortion law deterministic at the observed data and gives the zero-atom mass of the limiting law a direct reading as an effective-dimension proxy for the second-order information the filter has lost. Second, a regularized free deconvolution inverts the distortion with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and a computable forward residual certifies when the model behind it is violated. Injectivity makes the inverse identifiable but not stable, so the budget rests on a resolution-restricted condition number whose positivity we prove, and is vacuous below that resolution rather than concealed in a hypothesis. Third, the repaired spectrum enters only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so spectral error changes the mixing constants and not the invariant target, and the full cycle obeys a geometrically summable error recursion whose abstention term is governed by when abstentions fall rather than how many occur. Pre-registered simulations confirm the forward law, an order-of-magnitude reduction of spectral error, and the abstention law. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors.
  </details>

- **[Spectrum Is Not Enough: A Random-Matrix Account of Data-Free Preconditioning for Differentially Private Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21312)**  `arXiv:2610.21312`  
  _Shilin Zhang, Kangning Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  At a fixed privacy budget, curvature is exactly the object the budget makes unavailable. A recent answer estimates it from synthetic probes, at neither privacy cost nor distribution shift, and validates a probe by the eigenvalue decay it reproduces. That test reads the spectrum, not the basis, and what a probe reconstructs is unknown. This paper gives a random-matrix account of data-free preconditioning, organized by one dichotomy. Of the two Kronecker factors, the error-signal factor $ G $ and the architecture-determined bulk of the activation factor $ A $ are reconstructible without data up to an explicit error-energy bound; only the data-induced spikes of $ A $ are not. We verify that bound with zero violations along a full training trajectory, though it stays one to nearly three orders of magnitude above the gap it bounds. We locate the failure boundary at a Baik-Ben Arous-Péché threshold: a bulk-only probe suffers an exact damage $s^2/(1-s^2)$ from a spike of strength $s^2$, invisible once its amplitude exceeds the scaled-bulk threshold $( \sqrt {c}/(1+ \sqrt {c}))^{1/2}$, $c = d/n$. The test in use is basis-blind: rotating only the probe eigenbasis at a near-exact matched spectrum inflates the residual by $2.3 \times $ to $89.8 \times $, and a closed-form volume law fixes the within-spectrum ordering of the critical volume while a two-oracle construction proves that no functional of the probe spectrum fixes its magnitude. Over forty seeds on three modalities, per-layer tuning does not transfer to accuracy, no data-free arm beats the flat probe, public-data curvature does on both modalities tested, and the ordering inverts on PathMNIST under real DP noise. The account yields a probe-design protocol and falsifiable predictions for the regimes where data-free curvature can be trusted.
  </details>

- **[Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20585)**  `arXiv:2610.20585`  
  _Stavros Nousias, Akis Nousias, Konstantinos Gkrispanis_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31% and interior mean squared error by 47%.
  </details>

- **[Learning to Design SR Solvers: Harness Optimization for Symbolic Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16966)**  `arXiv:2610.16966`  
  _Qian Li, Yuxiao Hu, Qihao Duan, Jinyue Yan, Yuntian Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Symbolic regression (SR) seeks explicit equations that explain observed data, and recent methods increasingly employ large language models (LLMs) and agents for equation discovery. However, these systems typically rely on manually designed workflows and prompts. We argue that the SR agent harness should itself be an optimization target: its design shapes search priors and how numerical feedback guides subsequent equation refinement. We therefore propose HarnessSR, a framework for jointly optimizing prompts and workflows to construct reusable SR agents. During both harness optimization and agent execution, HarnessSR supports either PySR or an LLM-based equation generator through tool-specific interfaces, allowing the framework to optimize search guidance for different equation-discovery mechanisms. HarnessSR first optimizes role prompts through equation-discovery feedback in basic workflows, then jointly searches prompt assignments and workflows with brief adaptation to align the two. Finally, it refines role instructions through reflection on residual patterns, candidate equation structures, and search outcomes, improving how these signals guide subsequent equation search. On LSR-Synth in LLM-SRBench, HarnessSR achieves a mean ID $\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01}$ of 61.33% across three backbones, a 45.0% relative improvement over the next-best baseline.
  </details>

- **[DASS: A Solver-Adaptable Dynamic Auxiliary Search Strategy for Symbolic Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16812)**  `arXiv:2610.16812`  
  _Yuxiao Hu, Qian Li, Ding Wang, Yekun Zheng, Jinyue Yan, Yuntian Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Symbolic regression (SR) aims to discover interpretable mathematical expressions from data and plays a key role in scientific discovery. However, existing methods face a common bottleneck: the enormous search space and severe combinatorial explosion make it difficult to achieve a favorable trade-off between accuracy and algorithmic efficiency. We argue that, in addition to designing increasingly complex solver-specific SR strategies, an equally promising direction is to equip them with a shareable auxiliary strategy that can provide reliable search guidance. To this end, we propose DASS, a solver-adaptable Dynamic Auxiliary Search Strategy that improves SR by constructing and refining a high-potential auxiliary search subspace. DASS represents the auxiliary search space as a functional subspace spanned by a set of high-potential basis function terms. It estimates term utility through multi-environment evaluation, filters unstable guidance, and updates term potential scores with a Gibbs posterior, thereby calibrating the subspace to provide more reliable guidance for downstream solvers. The high-quality solutions produced by the solver are used to update the set of basis terms. This forms a virtuous closed-loop optimization process: the subspace guides the downstream solver, and the solver feedback reshapes the subspace for subsequent exploration. DASS can be easily integrated with various types of SR solvers. Extensive experiments on LLM-SRBench show that DASS significantly improves the accuracy of original solvers with a manageable increase in runtime.
  </details>

- **[Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens: Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16491)**  `arXiv:2610.16491`  
  _Xin Xu, Ke Cheng, Hao Wang, Yangru Huang, Yanghao Xiao, Zhichao Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version often exhausts the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. Inspired by the draft--verify principle of speculative decoding, we propose Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), a two-level framework coupling inner-loop agent search with outer-loop improver learning. SpecRSI drafts successors before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while adopting only fully evaluated, admissible versions. In the inner loop, Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. In the outer loop, Group Verification Optimization (GVO) updates the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. We evaluate SpecRSI on scientific optimization (including active queue management (AQM) for network infrastructure), coding, and general agent-system benchmarks. Under matched evaluation-call budgets, SpecRSI improves scientific terminal gain over Janus by 60.0%--96.3% and area under the budget curve by 32.1%--91.6%, while achieving higher means across all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and outperforming MetaRSI-v1 by 1.30--2.70 percentage points (pp) in system score across twenty backbones. On instance-level comparisons, it further improves PyBaMM terminal gain by 142.6% and SWE-Pro success by 6.0 pp at 7.0% and 9.2% lower token cost, respectively. These results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.
  </details>

- **[Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization: Unified Learning from Offline Demonstrations and On- and Off-Policy Rollouts via a Shared Regression Target](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12830)**  `arXiv:2610.12830`  
  _Du Cheng, Junyu Lu, Jingfan Zhang, Yuzhuo Zhang, Haoxuan Jia, Shichao Weng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reasoning post-training draws on offline demonstrations and policy-generated rollouts, yet conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) separates their objectives and limits continued reuse of collected responses. We propose \textbf{Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization} (CBPO), which makes these sources compatible with one regression loss through a fixed-reference target. Because the generating policy does not enter this target, positive and negative offline completions, reference responses, and current and historical rollouts can share a common reward-labeled record format and replay buffer. As new responses enter the buffer, optimization retains the same regression objective without coordinating separate SFT and RL objectives or requiring stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic. Restricting the available sources gives offline, on-policy, and off-policy variants, while CBPO-Unified combines them. Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO delivers leading \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} performance across benchmarks and data regimes. On Qwen3-1.7B, CBPO-Unified improves benchmark-averaged \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} over SFT DAPO by 2.33 and 4.44 percentage points, respectively. In the replay ablation, retaining historical rollouts improves these metrics by 1.87 and 3.72 percentage points over the no-history configuration.
  </details>

- **[SPIN: Shadow Predictive Indexer for Sparse Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09025)**  `arXiv:2610.09025`  
  _Yao Fu, Jiahan Chang, Yueying Li, Ritchie Zhao, Bryce Long, Mohammad Mahdi Kamani, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Indexer-based sparse attention reduces the cost of core attention by passing only a fixed, small number of important tokens to it. However, the indexer must still score the entire KV cache at every decoding step. This scoring overhead becomes a major bottleneck as the context length grows. We propose SPIN (Shadow Predictive Indexer) to reduce this indexer overhead. SPIN uses lightweight, history-based prediction to identify important KV blocks, avoiding the need to score the full KV cache at every decoding step. SPIN keeps the score history fresh with random exploration and allocates the block budget across layers by their measured miss rates. SPIN treats KV blocks and speculative decoding as first-class design and implementation considerations. Across extensive evaluations on long-context and agentic benchmarks, SPIN achieves 30-40% sparsity while preserving task quality. With larger exploration shares and per-layer block budgets, SPIN keeps task quality on the especially difficult MRCRv2 benchmark close to baseline at 50-57% effective block sparsity. In end-to-end vLLM serving, SPIN improves output throughput by up to 13.9% and reduces median inter-token latency by up to 13.6%.
  </details>

- **[ORCA: The Annealed Spectral Conditioning Optimizer for Faster, Better LLM Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06116)**  `arXiv:2610.06116`  
  _Yuanshi Liu, Boyuan Jiang, Liang Hou, Xin Tao, Pengfei Wan, Zhouchen Lin, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon's reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Why Does Train-Validation Separation Emerge? Update-Pressure Density Dynamics in Pretrained Backbones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01425)**  `arXiv:2610.01425`  
  _Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Ken-Tye Yong, Nguyen H. Tran_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  During fine-tuning, training accuracy often keeps improving after validation accuracy levels off, widening the train-validation gap. We propose a support-transfer account: early updates reuse structure shared by many examples, whereas later fitting relies on narrower structure whose benefits transfer less to held-out data. From fixed training examples, we normalize per-example gradient magnitudes over selected parameters and measure allocation dispersion across examples ($D_{\mathrm{den}}$) and within labels, weighted by class sample counts ($D_{\mathrm{within}}^{\mathrm{wt}}$). A local model gives sufficient conditions for dispersion and the cross-entropy gap to grow together, separating uniform score scaling; additional decision-boundary conditions characterize accuracy-gap growth. In a five-level hierarchy, increasing the share of private features, unique to individual examples, from 0.3 to 0.5 to 0.7 raises the final accuracy gap from 0.185 to 0.331 to 0.527 and increases unnormalized dispersion increments. Tests retaining one feature level at a time show a widening validation-minus-training difference in the private level's loss share. After the validation-loss minimum, the cross-entropy gap continues to grow without a decline in mean validation accuracy. Across 90 runs of RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and Qwen3-1.7B on six language tasks, both readouts correlate positively with the accuracy gap in every run; raw correlations of one-epoch changes are positive for $D_{\mathrm{den}}$ in 88/90 runs. Both readouts also retain positive associations in 15 ResNet-18 runs across three vision datasets. These results support a connection between evolving gradient allocation and train-validation separation.
  </details>

- **[Human-inspired, Task-Dimension-Guided Exploration for Efficient Learning in High Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36672)**  `arXiv:2609.36672`  
  _Fanyu Zhu, Jiahui An, Ni Ji_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Efficient exploration in high-dimensional decision spaces remains a central challenge for decision-making systems. Humans, in contrast, can navigate large decision spaces with remarkable efficiency. Recent behavioral studies suggest that humans reduce dimensionality in large decision spaces by probing candidate feature dimensions, identifying reward-relevant ones, and restricting the effective decision space. Inspired by this mechanism, we propose TDGE (Task-Dimension-Guided Exploration), a human-inspired, model-agnostic algorithm with an automatically constructed task-dimension--feature--item hierarchy. TDGE follows a top-down exploration strategy: it first selects task-relevant feature dimensions, then identifies informative features within those dimensions, and finally recommends concrete items based on the selected features. Experiments on MovieLens-20M, LastFM, and Amazon recommendation datasets show that TDGE substantially improves exploration efficiency and cold-start adaptation over baseline algorithms. Comparisons with other structured algorithms and ablation studies attribute these gains to TDGE's hierarchical structure and semantic feature-space exploration, with robust results across clustering methods and hierarchy depths. Recommendation-trajectory visualizations also show exploration patterns similar to human dimension-guided behavior.
  </details>

- **[ASTRA: ADMM-Accelerated Topology Reconfiguration for Dynamic Satellite Constellations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33993)**  `arXiv:2609.33993`  
  _João Norberto, Ricardo Ferreira, Cláudia Soares_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dynamic topology reconfiguration is central to the reliability and efficiency of large satellite constellations, yet many existing approaches rely on idealized assumptions such as full constellation deployment or uniform orbital spacing. We present Adaptive Satellite Topology via Regret-Aware learning (ASTRA), a theoretically grounded framework for dynamic satellite topology reconfiguration that builds on an online learning formulation and makes it computationally practical. ASTRA combines an ADMM-based offline solver with efficient online updates for both online gradient descent and online conditional gradient, yielding markedly cheaper constrained updates than generic optimization pipelines. On the theory side, we show that for a relevant class of entry-wise nonzero utility matrices, the objective is strongly convex, which yields logarithmic static regret for online gradient descent, and we further instantiate known dynamic-regret guarantees under inexact ADMM inner loops. Empirically, ASTRA matches or improves topology quality, presenting a good trade-off with computational time on synthetic constellations, and it remains effective on real Starlink data under partial deployment and non-uniform spacing, where idealized structural assumptions break down. These results position ASTRA as an efficient and theoretically grounded approach to topology reconfiguration in realistic Low Earth Orbit networks.
  </details>

- **[Counterfactual Online Conformal Prediction Under Adaptive Logging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30811)**  `arXiv:2609.30811`  
  _Xinyu Qiao, Yichen Lin, Kaihong Ji, Xue Wang, Tao Yao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Online conformal prediction can fail when predictions shape actions and actions determine which outcomes enter calibration. Standard adaptive methods may retain marginal coverage while systematically miscovering the counterfactual outcomes of rarely selected actions. This paper formalizes the failure through counterfactual coverage and introduces Propensity-Weighted Online Conformal Prediction, an inverse-propensity-weighted recursion that debiases calibration. A doubly robust variant further reduces nuisance bias to the product of outcome-model and propensity errors. Under positivity and known logging probabilities, both methods attain the minimax expected coverage rate for nondegenerate calibration. Experiments on synthetic decision tasks, Open Bandit data, and financial rebalancing demonstrate counterfactual coverage gains under selection-biased logging, with prediction-set widths close to those of the oracle in the reported sharpness study.
  </details>

- **[Learning Risk Scores Robust to Unobserved Confounders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27144)**  `arXiv:2609.27144`  
  _Ryan Edmonds, Yingxiao Ye, Sina Aghaei, Andrés Gómez, Çağıl Koçyiğit, Phebe Vayanos_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We consider the problem of learning risk scores to prioritize individuals for scarce resources or interventions, from historical observational data affected by unobserved confounding. Decisions about who receives scarce resources are often guided by risk scores based on recorded characteristics, such as responses to a survey. These risk scores are increasingly being learned directly from observational data: historical records of individuals' characteristics, allocation decisions, and outcomes. Standard methods such as inverse propensity weighting (IPW), which corrects for the bias introduced by the historical allocation policy, can be used to learn accurate risk scores if the historical decision process is fully explained by the recorded characteristics. In practice, however, historical decisions often depend on unrecorded information, causing learned risk scores to systematically under-prioritize exactly the individuals whose unrecorded circumstances drove past prioritization. We propose a method for learning risk scores that are robust to this kind of unobserved confounding, building on IPW. Since propensity weights cannot be reliably estimated under unobserved confounding, we instead treat them as belonging to an uncertainty set determined by the observable data and domain-informed estimates of the degree of confounding, combining sensitivity analysis from causal inference with Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization. The resulting robust risk score learning problem admits a sample-based approximation that we reformulate as an exponential cone program compatible with off-the-shelf solvers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on semi-synthetic data derived from datasets in the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Our method improves calibration by up to 29.2% over traditional benchmarks and up to 11.1% over the state of the art, without compromising other metrics.
  </details>

- **[Riemannian Neural Hamiltonian Flows: From Interpretable Potentials to Exact Surrogate Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21647)**  `arXiv:2609.21647`  
  _Vincent Souveton_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Hamiltonian normalizing flows are attractive generative models because their phase-space maps are invertible and volume preserving, but most neural constructions are formulated in Euclidean space. We introduce Riemannian Neural Hamiltonian Flows, which combine the fixed kinetic energy of a Riemannian manifold, a learned scalar potential, and an explicit geodesic integrator. We then study the interpretability of the learned potential through a thermodynamic reading in which the momentum variance plays the role of a temperature. The matched potential, whose Boltzmann distribution is the data, is the potential whose force balances the pressure of the data. The output of one pass of the flow is the Boltzmann distribution of the learned potential multiplied by a memory factor, so that the learned potential is the matched potential whenever the pass forgets its starting point. Numerical experiments on Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical spaces show competitive sample quality and numerical cost against a Riemannian continuous normalizing flow, and confirm the interpretability of the learned potential. We then show that this reading has a computational use. When the energy of the data is known but expensive, the landscape learned from existing samples is a surrogate energy for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, allowing exact sampling with significant acceleration. We test this approach on the localization of a neutrino source from public IceCube data.
  </details>

- **[Physical-State-Guided Diffusion Sampling for Full-Waveform Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12899)**  `arXiv:2609.12899`  
  _Chen Min, Haowen Jiang, Zheng Ma, Xiong-Bin Yan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Full waveform inversion (FWI) reconstructs subsurface velocity models from seismic mea surements but faces the challenges of ill-posedness and nonlinearity, making accurate inversion dependent on suitable initialization and effective prior constraints. Classical methods stabi lize the inversion and improve convergence by designing hand-crafted regularization terms, yet these terms provide limited descriptions of complex geological structures. Recent diffusion based methods learn more detailed structural priors from data and integrate them into inverse problem solvers. We propose Physical-State-Guided Diffusion Sampling (PSG), which decouples diffusion posterior sampling into two mutually interacting processes: regularized FWI optimiza tion and conditional diffusion sampling with linear guidance. PSG shows overall improvements in reconstruction accuracy, preservation of prior structure, and robustness over classical and diffusion-based baselines across diverse OpenFWI inversion scenarios. Through domain decom position, PSG can generalize without retraining to more complex, realistic velocity fields with structural patterns distinct from those represented by the prior learned from training datasets and larger spatial domains than the training models. Overall, PSG offers a flexible framework for integrating learned priors with physical constraints, with potential for extension to other nonlinear inverse problems.
  </details>

- **[Temporal-Causal Inference for Reinforcement Learning via Automata Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07461)**  `arXiv:2609.07461`  
  _Jan Corazza, Daniil Kaminskyi, Simon Lutz, Patrick Nossol, Hadi Partovi Aria, Zhe Xu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We consider reinforcement learning in environments with dynamics that undergo an irreversible phase transition governed by a hidden temporal pattern. The agent observes the base state but cannot observe the phase directly. We formalize this problem as a two-phase non-Markovian decision process and introduce Temporal-Causal Inference for Reinforcement Learning (TCIRL), a framework that jointly learns a control policy and infers the hidden temporal cause of the phase transition. TCIRL maintains a hypothesis deterministic finite automaton (DFA) to track what phase is active and refines it via counterexample-driven SAT-based synthesis. We prove that the hypothesis converges almost surely to a DFA whose language induces the same dynamics as the cause language, yielding an optimal policy for the original non-Markovian decision process. Experiments on a genetic therapy gridworld and a traffic signal environment show that TCIRL recovers the correct cause DFA and matches the full-information baseline in both domains.
  </details>

- **[NashDreamer: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01549)**  `arXiv:2609.01549`  
  _Tomáš Holeček, Viliam Lisý_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has achieved remarkable results in single-agent domains, yet its extension to competitive imperfect information games (IIGs) remains underexplored. In multi-agent settings, opponent-induced non-stationarity complicates the learning process, and decentralized model learning faces severe identifiability barriers, which we argue make centralized model learning a mathematical necessity. Building on this analysis, we propose NashDreamer, a principled MBRL framework for two-player zero-sum IIGs. It introduces a centralized Multi-Agent Recurrent State-Space Model (MARSSM) that decouples environment dynamics from the effect of players' strategies on their individual observations. NashDreamer is designed to use arbitrary policy gradient algorithms and inherits their convergence guarantees towards Nash equilibria under an idealized model. Empirical evaluations across five benchmark games demonstrate that NashDreamer substantially improves sample efficiency over model-free baselines early in the training. Finally, we theoretically analyze the architecture's optimization landscape, identifying the vulnerability of the Dreamer family of algorithms to posterior collapse in stochastic environments. We leave it as an open challenge.
  </details>

- **[CRAD: Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation for Decentralized Heterogeneous Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00446)**  `arXiv:2609.00446`  
  _Baraa Bilbeisi, Mengchen Fan, Baocheng Geng, Qing Tian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Conventional federated learning (FL) relies on parameter averaging, which forces clients to be doubly homogeneous: it demands an identical architecture and degrades under non-IID data. Real-world deployments usually break both assumptions. We sidestep both by building a decentralized knowledge distillation framework in which each client evaluates its peers' model snapshots on its own local data and distills from the resulting soft predictions. Because knowledge is transferred through the shared class posterior, clients are free to run different architectures; and because every teacher is evaluated on the student's own device, raw data never leaves the client, with no central server or public dataset required. Within this setting, we identify and address an under-examined problem: how to combine the peer teacher predictions. Existing methods, like uniform averaging, ignore how knowledge reliability varies across teachers and classes. We propose Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation (CRAD), which, per class, first discards teachers that disagree with the peer consensus and then takes a weighted average of the rest, weighting each teacher by its per-class reliability (precision, or inverse variance). Since the variance of an accuracy from $n$ samples scales as $1/n$, support enters automatically: among the teachers that survive filtering, a teacher is trusted for a class to the degree that it is both accurate and well-evidenced for it. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and PathMNIST, across heterogeneous architectures under severe non-IID skew, CRAD consistently outperforms competing methods in global accuracy. Our code is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[On the Indistinguishability of Human v/s AI Generated Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26797)**  `arXiv:2608.26797`  
  _Jaee Ponde, Aritra Das, Mihir More, Debayan Gupta_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The rapid improvement of LLMs has made distinguishing AI-generated text from human writing a pressing problem. This challenge is further amplified by paraphrasing tools designed to make machine-generated text appear more ``human''. We study how access to human writing samples can be used to strategically paraphrase machine-generated responses toward the human distribution. Under a multi-sample setting with human and machine responses to the same prompts, we show that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward a human target under mixing and stability conditions. We derive an explicit convergence rate, examine how semantic-preservation and quality constraints affect this rate, and extend the analysis to finite samples to characterize how the required human data and paraphrasing rounds scale with the desired error. We extend the analysis beyond the shared-parameter setting by learning a human-preserving rewriting kernel.
  </details>

- **[Functional compatibility as a determinant of persistent neural learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22462)**  `arXiv:2608.22462`  
  _Hossein Javidnia_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Neural networks can acquire new capabilities while damaging existing ones, but what determines whether new learning persists remains unclear. We identify functional compatibility, the extent to which incoming learning can coexist with behaviour that must be preserved, as an experimentally manipulable causal determinant of persistence. From identical neural states, we vary compatibility while matching unrestricted learning opportunity and imposing a common retention requirement. Persistent learning increases with compatibility across independent directions, convolutional and transformer architectures, vision and text, and a ten-seed replication. Learning rules and retention constraints determine how much compatible opportunity is retained, whereas nonlinear geometry limits the matched intervention at larger update norms. Functional compatibility therefore reframes stability-plasticity from preventing forgetting to determining which new learning can coexist with existing function and persist.
  </details>

- **[Advancing Open and Reproducible Relational Learning: RelArena-$α$, TabPFN-Rel and RPI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16319)**  `arXiv:2608.16319`  
  _Adrian Hayler, Klemens Flöge, Alan Arazi, Rishabh Ranjan, Jure Leskovec, Felix Birkel, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This first release of Prior Labs in relational learning shows our continued commitment to open science. We open-source three pieces of software that we expect to accelerate research in the field towards meaningful real-world impact. We aim to steer further development based on feedback from, and in collaboration with, the community. Given the early stage of development, our $\alpha$-release targets researchers and early-adopting practitioners. Over the past years, a variety of datasets and tasks for relational learning have emerged, but the community has not converged on a reliable, reproducible way to compare different methods on these tasks. Our $\alpha$-release, RelArena-$\alpha$, provides a unified framework for running and comparing baselines on RelBench v1 by standardizing data loading, evaluation protocols, tuning regimes, and support for systems with custom tuning, inspired by established tabular benchmarks such as TabArena. We plan to work with the research community to further develop RelArena-$\alpha$ into a catalyst for progress in the relational learning community. We release the initial version of TabPFN-Rel, a purpose-built relational harness for TabPFN-3. Currently ranked first among models on RelArena-$\alpha$, TabPFN-Rel makes key improvements upon RDBLearn. Beyond its ranking, TabPFN-Rel serves as a strong baseline, adding to the growing evidence that flattening a relational database into a single table remains competitive with specialized relational architectures on real-world tasks.To facilitate adoption of relational learning methods in research and industry, we release an initial $\alpha$-version of our Relational Predictive Interface, RPI, an open-source, model-agnostic interface that enables early adopters to easily define problems on new databases and apply any model implemented in RelArena-$\alpha$, including TabPFN-Rel, to these problems.
  </details>

- **[DACRI: Decision-Aware Causal Intervention Ranking for Critical Supply Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11154)**  `arXiv:2608.11154`  
  _Shiqi Huang, Jiani He, Dingyan Shang, Yihua Xu, Jize Li, Yan Lyu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Detecting or attributing a supply-chain disruption is not the same as selecting the intervention that maximizes recoverable net value. We present CriticalSCM-Bench v1, a controlled synthetic benchmark with causal ground truth, paired factual/counterfactual rollouts, and an explicit net-value objective. Relative to a full-information train-selected static benchmark, LambdaMART improves median normalized net value by 5.7--16.2\%, with paired statistical support on the semiconductor and critical-material archetypes but not on digital infrastructure. On digital infrastructure, a domain-informed constant-buffer policy remains stronger, showing that greater model complexity is not uniformly justified. Across partial and delayed settings, LambdaMART retains 33--75\% of full-clamp value. Stress tests further show that intervention fidelity, timing, cost, and held-out disruptions can alter policy ordering. Critical materials show the weakest out-of-distribution retention. Separately, a guarded explanation study over 540 generations preserves every fixed intervention decision after deterministic validation and template fallback, although exact wording remains unstable. Within this controlled setting, the results identify regimes in which adaptive ranking adds value and those in which simpler structural policies remain preferable.
  </details>

- **[Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning for Genomics Applications: Insights from an Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11054)**  `arXiv:2608.11054`  
  _Sepideh Saran, Mahsa Ghanbari, Uwe Ohler_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep learning models have emerged as the standard computational tool for a wide range of applications in genomics. Yet, uncertainty quantification (UQ) --- and more specifically, the reliability of different uncertainty estimates in this domain --- has received little systematic attention. This work presents an empirical analysis of UQ in deep learning models, focusing on genomics applications.
